TRIBIWNLYS PRISIO CYMRU  -  VALUATION TRIBUNAL FOR WALES

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 1 of 7

Appellant: Thomas E Teague agent for Jon Durran (Occupier)

Appellant’s Address: White Lion Inn, Bank Street, Chepstow NP16 5EL

Appeal number: 684028927561/192NV17

The Matter Appealed against: 2017 Rating List

Date of Hearing: Friday 21st September 2018

Appearances: Mr John Keane (agent for the occupier), Mr Greg Overs (for
the respondent Valuation Officer)

Date of Decision: 15th October 2018

Decision of Tribunal: Appeal allowed in part

Members of the Tribunal: Mrs E Price-Suter (Chairperson), Mr T Cook, Mr R
Henley

Tribunal Clerk: Mr G Harris

Introduction

1. This is a summary of the case and is not intended to be an exhaustive
record of the proceedings. However, the parties can be assured that all
the evidence was fully considered by the tribunal when it arrived at its
decision. Consequently, the absence of reference to any statement, or
evidence, should not be construed as being overlooked.

Summary of the Case

2. Mr Keane explained that the matter for consideration by the tribunal
related to a 2017 compiled list appeal in respect of The White Lion Inn,
Chepstow. The appellant contended that the Rateable Value (RV) was too
high at £42,900 and should be reduced to £23,000 with effect from 1st
April 2017.
3. Mr Keane stated that the appeal property was a Grade II listed public
house dating from 1644. It was situated in the centre of Chepstow at the
junction of Bank Street and High Street facing a small square. It was of
traditional stone and brick construction under a multi-pitched tiled roof and
had wooden framed single glazed windows. To the rear was a paved
patio area containing approximately 6 picnic benches.

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 2 of 7
4. The internal trade accommodation comprised a public bar, a rear late
night bar and a coffee shop. Each trade area had a distinct demographic
profile with the public bar being favoured by those in the 35-50 bracket,
the late night bar by 18-25’s and the coffee shop by a more mature
clientele and shoppers.
5. Mr Keane explained that the layout of the pub was quite dispersed with a
central passage effectively separating the coffee shop from the rest of the
property. Consequently, staffing costs were high with an inevitable
element of duplication, these costs had been reflected in the working
expenses of the business. The White Lion had a late licence to serve
alcohol until 1:00am at weekends and could stay open until 1:30. The
premises licence, a copy of which was attached in the appendixes to his
evidence pack, included a mandatory condition to employ door staff
during alcohol sales hours, with the extra costs incurred itemised as a
separate expense in Mr Keane’s valuation.
6. Mr Keane explained that the basis of valuation was set down under
Paragraph 2(1) Schedule 6 of the Local Government Finance Act 1988,
as amended. It was defined as an amount equal to the rent at which it is
estimated the hereditament might reasonably be expected to let from year
to year on the assumptions that -
(a)  the tenancy begins on the day by reference to which the
determination is to be made;
(b)  immediately before the tenancy begins the hereditament is in a state
of reasonable repair, but excluding from this assumption any repairs
which a reasonable landlord would consider uneconomic; and
(c)  the tenant undertakes to pay all usual tenant’s rates and taxes and to
bear the cost of the repairs and insurance and the other expenses (if
any) necessary to maintain the hereditament in a state to command
the rent mentioned above.
For the purposes of this appeal the Antecedent Valuation Date (AVD) was
1st April 2015.
7. Mr Keane stated that the usual methodology for the valuation of public
houses was contained in The Approved Guide to the Valuation of Public
Houses (“the guide”) a copy of which was attached in the appendixes to
his evidence pack. The valuation approach was to estimate the Fair
Maintainable Trade (FMT) of the hereditament, broken down into wet,
food, accommodation and other, and apply a percentage “bid” to each of
those income streams with the resultant figure representing the rateable
value. The Guide divided the country into 3 areas – Central London, Outer
London and Provincial England and Wales and each area into 3 bands –
Category 1 (Upper), Category 2 (Middle) and Category 3 (Lower). There
were 2 bands for food sales – A (Upper) and B (Lower). It was the task of
the valuer to place the hereditament in question into this matrix. In this
case the valuer had placed The White Lion at the bottom of Category 3 for
wet sales and the bottom of Band B for food sales. Mr Keane believed
those choices were constrained by the Guide and contended that the
resulting RV was still too high.

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 3 of 7
8. Referring to Case Law, Mr Keane highlighted the case Sharp v Griffiths
(VO) 1992 where Mr Norman Rose stated that the Guide is, in effect “a
truncated profits method” of valuation that had no statutory basis and was
not binding on individuals or the Valuation Tribunal. In the more recent
Valuation Tribunal for England case Brown v Kirk (VO) the President of
the Tribunal said “the guide is what it says it is, merely a guide, a degree
of subjective decision making is still required of the valuer or on appeal
the Tribunal”. It was Mr Keane’s opinion that the Guide was not flexible
enough to adequately reflect the actual circumstances of The White Lion,
specifically the high wage costs and the expense of employing door staff
and as such a more refined approach was necessary.
9. Mr Keane contended that as the Guide was a “truncated profits method”
that it was appropriate, therefore to use the full profits method to provide a
more nuanced valuation. Mr Keane stated that the profits method was an
established method for the valuation of public houses, although had been
used less frequently since the introduction of the Guide and the insistence
by the Valuation Office on its use.
10. Mr Keane explained the principles behind the profits method and stated
that the starting point was an assessment of the Fair Maintainable Trade
(FMT). Mr Keane had provided the Valuation Officer with detailed Profit
and Loss accounts for the years ending 30th June 2015 and 30th June
2016, copies of which were attached to his appendixes. In this case the
FMT at the AVD had been agreed between the parties as being £408,000
for wet sales and ££42,000 for food sales, being the approximate average
of the 2015 and 2016 trades. For consistency Mr Keane had adopted
approximate averages of the working expenses for his valuation and
commented that the gross profit was in line with market expectations and
as far as he was aware was accepted as reasonable by the Valuation
Officer. Mr Keane’s valuation was as follows –

11. Mr Keane explained that according to the 2016 Cost Guide for Tied
Tenants and Lessees to the Running of a Pub, a copy of which was
attached in the appendixes to his evidence, the average working
expenses expressed as a percentage of turnover for this type of public
house was 33%. The actual working expenses of the White Lion were
43% of turnover, significantly more than the upper end of the range in the
2016 Cost Guide. This disparity was attributable to the exceptional costs
of employing staff and door security. This was reflective of the fact that
the appeal property had 3 distinct trade areas, all of which needed to be
staffed. In addition, door staff had to be employed according to the terms
outlined in the Premises Licence.

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 5 of 7
12. In conclusion, Mr Keane contended that the Approved Guide did not
reflect the exceptional circumstances of The White Lion due to its physical
layout and additional staffing requirements coupled with the legal
requirements to employ door staff which resulted in significantly higher
working expenses than those at the upper end of the licenced trade’s
benchmarking tool. A full profits method valuation provided a more
nuanced valuation which was better able to reflect the individual
advantages and disadvantages of The White Lion. In light of this, Mr
Keane asked that the Tribunal confirm a RV of £23,000.
13. Under cross examination Mr Keane confirmed that he had not departed
from using the Guide in any other valuation of a public house. Mr Keane
explained that the current occupier’s sister had signed the original
tenancy on 1st February 2010 for a period of 15 years with preordained 3
yearly rent reviews. The original rent was for £52,000 per annum, rising to
£60,000 in 2013, £68,000 on the 2nd review, £73,000 on the 3rd and
£83,000 on the 4th. It was Mr Keane’s opinion that the rent was
unsustainable. The current occupier had inherited the lease when his
sister had passed away.
14. Mr Overs, for the Valuation Officer, introduced the appeal property and
provided the Tribunal with external photographs and a plan of its layout.
He explained that it had been entered into the 2017 Rating List at a RV of
£42,900 with effect from 1st April 2017. It had been valued according to
Paragraph 2(1) Schedule 6 of the Local Government Finance Act 1988.
15. Mr Overs explained that public houses, bars and inns were valued on a
rental basis. Traditional public houses use “fair maintainable turnover” as
the comparator to assist in the analysis of rental evidence and therefore
as a valuation basis. Percentage rental bids were then applied to the
various income streams making up the FMT depending on location, age,
modernity, style of operation etc. as set out in the Valuation of Public
Houses Approved Guide.
16. Mr Overs stated that The Pubs Rating Forum had been established in
2014 in order to provide a vehicle through which the pub industry and the
Valuation Office Agency could maintain an on-going dialogue and
exchange of information in respect of matters relevant to the valuation for
rating of public houses. The forum included the following member
organisations –
•
British Beer & Pub Association
•
Association of Licensed Multiple Retailers
•
British Institute of Innkeeping
•
Federation of Licensed Victuallers Associations
•
Guild of Master Victuallers
17. In collaboration with the Forum and its appointed rating advisers (Gerald
Eve, Lawrence Tattersall, BNP Paribas and Davis Coffer Lyons) the
available rental evidence had been analysed and considered in detail,
along with other market performance indicators. The Approved Guide had

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 6 of 7
been agreed with the Forum, following a period of 4 months intensive
discussions covering all relevant factors.
18. Mr Overs explained that the Guide had been used to value all of the
public houses (over 44,000) in England and Wales for the 2017 Rating
List and to his knowledge the VOA had not departed from the Guide in the
defence and settlement of any public house rating appeal.
19. Mr Overs believed that the analysis of the accounts used by Mr Keane in
his valuation showed a healthy income for the property but that the
outgoings appeared exceptionally high giving a low profit margin and
hence a low amount available for rent and rates. Mr Overs contended that
to depart from the Guide in considering the RV of a public house
consideration had also to be made to the actual rent passing on the
property which was stated to be £60,000 with effect from 25th June 2014.
After deducting an amount to represent the domestic element of the
property, the resulting figure would provide a high assessment not
consistent with similar pubs in the locality trading at a similar FMT.
20. Therefore, Mr Overs believed that the only consistent approach to arriving
at the correct RV for the appeal property was to follow the approved
guide. Referring to the Guide, Mr Overs had considered each category
and band and having had regard to the particular disabilities of the
property had adopted the minimum category of both bands for wet and
food trades. In particular he had taken into account the front and rear bars
and the separate shop type premises within the curtilage which required
additional staffing and running costs above the average, and also the
additional door security costs as indicated in the accounts. Mr Over’s

21. In conclusion, Mr Overs urged the tribunal not to depart from using the
Approved Guide in considering the correct RV for The White Lion Inn. In
using the Guide and having regard to the particular disadvantages of the
property, adopting the minimum of the lowest band adequately reflected
the particular hereditament whilst maintaining a consistent approach to
the valuation of public houses. Adopting the minimum of the lowest bands
to the agreed FMT had given a RV of £34,000 with effect from 1st April
2017 which he asked the Tribunal to confirm.

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 7 of 7
22. Under cross examination, Mr Overs believed the rent to be exceptionally
high and not useful as it had been agreed 5 years prior to the AVD
although all evidence was considered depending upon its weight. Mr
Overs agreed that the property was unique but did not believe that this
was enough reason to depart from the Guide, stating that lots of public
houses have more than 2 bars and other pubs in Chepstow employ door
staff.
23. At the conclusion of the hearing, the tribunal decided to reserve its
decision.

The Reasons for Decision

24. Having considered all the evidence placed before it the tribunal decided
as follows: -

25. The Tribunal accepted that there was no dispute between the parties with
regard to the FMT used by each party in their respective valuations. The
dispute centred upon the method of valuation used to obtain the RV of the
hereditament.

26. Mr Keane contended that due to the exceptional circumstances of The
White Lion due to its physical layout and additional staffing requirements,
a full profits method valuation would provide a more nuanced valuation
which was better able to reflect the individual advantages and
disadvantages of hereditament. Mr Overs on the other hand contended
that the property should be valued in accordance with The Approved
Guide to the Valuation of Public Houses.

27. The Tribunal whilst acknowledging that the full profits method could be
used in the valuation of a public house believed that such guidance such
as The Approved Guide, agreed by the VOA and on behalf of a particular
category of ratepayers, in this case The Pubs Rating Forum, ought to be
followed unless there was good reason not to. The Tribunal accepted that
The White Lion Inn had unconventional layout which had resulted in high
staffing costs however did not consider this to be unique in the public
house industry and therefore was not reason enough to depart from The
Approved Guide.

28. The Tribunal was satisfied that Mr Overs had adequately reflected the
characteristics of the appeal property when deciding in which category
and band to place it for his valuation and that his proposed RV of £34,000
was fair and reasonable.  In light of this, the Tribunal orders the Valuation
Officer to amend the RV of The White Lion Inn, Bank Street, Chepstow
NP16 5EL to £34,000 with effect from 1st April 2017.

text:
TRIBIWNLYS PRISIO CYMRU  -  VALUATION TRIBUNAL FOR WALES

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 1 of 5

Appellant: Mrs E G Skov-Newton

Appellant’s Address: 35 Moor Street, Chepstow NP16 5DE

Appeal number: 684029031553/192NV17

The Matter Appealed against: 2017 Rating List

Date of Hearing: Friday 21st September 2018

Appearances: Mr G Overs (for the respondent Valuation Officer)

Date of Decision: 18th October 2018

Decision of Tribunal: Appeal allowed in part

Members of the Tribunal: Mrs E Price-Suter (Chairperson), Mr T Cook, Mr R
Henley

Tribunal Clerk: Mr G Harris

Introduction:

1. Mrs Skov-Newton contended, in a proposal to alter an entry in the 2017
Rating List received by the Valuation Officer on 5th May 2017, that the
Rateable Value (RV) of 35 Moor Street, Chepstow was incorrect and
should be reduced from £10,500 to £7,000 with effect from 1st April 2017.

2. This is a summary of the case and is not intended to be an exhaustive
record of the proceedings. However, the parties can be assured that all
the evidence was fully considered by the tribunal when it arrived at its
decision. Consequently, the absence of reference to any statement, or
evidence, should not be construed as being overlooked.

Summary of the Case

3. Prior to the hearing Mrs Skov-Newton had indicated that she had been
unable to attend and requested that the panel hear and determine the
appeal in her absence. In light of this the clerk presented Mrs Skov-
Newton’s submission to the panel.
4. In her submission Mrs Skov-Newton described how the RV of the appeal
property had increased from £6,600 in the 2010 Rating List to £10,500
upon revaluation for the 2017 Rating List, an increase of £3,900. Mrs

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 2 of 5
Skov-Newton had believed that the RV was based on achievable rent,
which had been confirmed to her in a letter from Mr Overs in which he had
written –
“The rateable value of a non-domestic hereditament none of which
consists of domestic property and none of which is exempt from non-
domestic rating shall be taken to be an amount equal to the rent at which
it is estimated the hereditament might reasonably be expected to let from
year to year.”
Mrs Skov-Newton contended that to expect a rental value of £10,500 for a
shop the size of 35 Moor Street was simply not achievable. She estimated
that a more realistic value would be £6,000/£7,000 in 2018’s retail
environment.
5. Mrs Skov-Newton explained that to be able to justify a rateable value per
m2 you had to know and understand the town and the location of premises
related to footfall and attractiveness and not just look at a street map. Mrs
Skov-Newton referred to St Mary Street which she said was a prime
location and a very attractive pedestrian street that adjoined High Street. It
contained a number of small retail units, cafes and pubs and where the
level of value was £155/£255. She highlighted13 St Mary Street as being
the same size as the appeal property but with a rate of £155/m2, 19 St
Mary Street had the same rate.
6. Mrs Skov-Newton explained that Moor Street had been called by town
councillors the ‘dead end’ of Chepstow, it was located ‘above the Town
Arch’ away from the High Street. Her property, located further from the
town centre, had been valued using £270/m2 whilst properties closer to the
Town Arch/High Street with a larger footfall had a lower value of £230/m2.
Mrs Skov-Newton questioned the correctness of the difference in values.
7. In addition, 4 retail units in Thomas Street, opposite the entrance to Marks
and Spencer some 65m from the appeal property had been valued using
£150/m2.
8. Mrs Skov-Newton stated that since the unfair increase in Business Rates
there had been an alarming closure of retail shops in Chepstow, in the last
2 months there had been 5 closures including the Herbert Lewis
department store which had operated in Chepstow for 170 years.
Independent retailers like her were fighting on all fronts against falling
footfall due to on-line shopping and out-of-town shopping centres and now
unrealistic business rates.
9. Mr Overs, for the Valuation Officer, introduced the appeal property and
described it as being located towards the top end of Moor Street with rear
access to the shop from Thomas Street. He provided the Tribunal with
external photographs, a map of its location and a plan of its layout
together with the Valuation Officer’s survey details. It had been entered
into the 2017 Rating List at a RV of £10,500 with effect from 1st April
2017. He explained that the basis of valuation for the appeal property had

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 3 of 5
been defined under Paragraph 2(1) Schedule 6 of the Local Government
Finance Act 1988 as –
2(1) The rateable value of a non-domestic hereditament [none of which
consists of domestic property and none of which is exempt from non-
domestic rating] shall be take to be an amount equal to the rent at which
it is estimated the hereditament might reasonably be expected to let from
year to year on these three assumptions-
(a) the first assumption is that the tenancy begins on the day by reference
to which the determination is to be made;
(b) the second assumption is that immediately before the tenancy begins
the hereditament is in a state of reasonable repair, but excluding from
this assumption any repairs which a reasonable landlord would
consider uneconomic;
(c) the third assumption is that the tenant undertakes to pay all usual
tenant’s rates and taxes and to bear the cost of the repairs and
insurance and the other expenses (if any) necessary to maintain the
hereditament in a state to command the rent mentioned above.
10. Mr Overs explained that statute further required that the property must be
valued by reference to values pertaining as at 1st April 2015 but having
regard to the physical state of the property and its physical setting as at
the material day, in this case 1st April 2017. Mr Overs valuation of the

12. Mr Overs explained that the rear access to Thomas Street with Marks and
Spencer and a car park could possibly have generated footfall and hence
a higher zone A value of £270/m2. In light of this Mr Overs requested that
the tribunal confirm a RV of £10,500 in respect of 35 Moor Street.
13. At the conclusion of the hearing, the tribunal decided to reserve its
decision.

The Reasons for Decision

14. Having considered all the evidence placed before it the tribunal decided as
follows: -

15. In her proposal Mrs Skov-Newton had contended that the Rating List was
inaccurate and that the RV of the appeal property should be reduced to
£7,000 with effect from 1st April 2017.

16. In cases such as this the tribunal had to initially consider the rental
evidence available on the appeal property or on comparable properties
within its locality. In the absence of direct rental evidence on the appeal
property as it was owner occupied the tribunal had looked at rents that
transpired on Moor Street as a whole. Considering the weight of evidence,
the tribunal placed less weight on the majority rental evidence provided by
Mr Overs as they had transpired too far away from the AVD of 1st April
2015 and needed to be adjusted accordingly. Similarly, the tribunal placed
little weight on the rent at 5 Moor Street as Mr Overs had stated that it had
been signed between connected parties and the rent at 9 Moor Street,
although effective from 1st August 2015, had been agreed following a rent
review the terms of which had not been specified.

17. The tribunal placed more weight on the passing rent and settlement
evidence at 16B Moor Street with the rent effective from 1st October 2015
and a resulting agreement on appeal of a zone A value of £230/m2.  This
was further supported by Mrs Skov-Newton’s contentions that the zone A

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 5 of 5
rate applied at both St Mary’s Street and Thomas Street was lower than
Moor Street, which had not been disputed by Mr Overs.
18. The tribunal accepted that in valuing properties within a town centre the
usual practice employed by valuers reflected the fact that higher zone A
values applied to properties closer to the city centre thus reflected their
positions as being in a more advantageous trading location. In this case,
the tribunal believed that the location of the appeal property being further
from the city centre warranted a zone A value more on par with that
ascribed to the lower end of Moor Street. Hence £230/m2 was considered
by the tribunal to be a more suitable amount.

19. Taking into account the tribunals decision that the zone A value of

title: 685529893990/192NV17: 91, Brynymor Road, Swansea, SA1 4JG
text:
TRIBIWNLYS PRISIO CYMRU  -  VALUATION TRIBUNAL FOR WALES

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 1 of 3

Appellant: Mr Daniel Carman

Appellant’s Address: 91 Brynymor Road, Swansea SA1 4JG

Appeal number: 685529893990/192NV17/40

The Matter Appealed against: 2017 Rating List

Date of Hearing: Thursday 8th November 2018

Appearances: Mr D Carman (Appellant) & Mr A Morse (for the respondent
Valuation Officer)

Date of Decision:  22nd November 2018

Decision of Tribunal: Appeal allowed in part

Members of the Tribunal: Mr B Al-Khanchi (Chairman), Mrs A Wingrave &
Mrs LM Thomas

Tribunal Clerk: Mr G Harris

Introduction:
1. Mr Carman contended in a proposal to alter an entry in the 2017 Rating
List, received by the Valuation Officer on 16th October 2017 that the
Rateable Value (RV) of 91 Brynymor Road, Swansea was incorrect and
should be reduced from £14,250 to £11,960 with effect from 1st April
2017.
2. This is a summary of the case and is not intended to be an exhaustive
record of the proceedings. However, the parties can be assured that all
the evidence was fully considered by the tribunal when it arrived at its
decision. Consequently, the absence of reference to any statement, or
evidence, should not be construed as being overlooked.

Summary of the Case

3. Mr Carman explained that he operated a small independent laundrette
and was under a lot of pressure. The RV was currently £14,250 and a

title: 681528927088/541NV17: 120, Woodville Road, Cardiff, CF24 4EE
text:
TRIBIWNLYS PRISIO CYMRU  -  VALUATION TRIBUNAL FOR WALES

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 1 of 5

Appellant: Mr John Winter

Appellant’s Address: 120 Woodville Road, Cardiff CF24 4EE

Appeal number: 681528927088/541NV17

The Matter Appealed against: 2017 Rating List

Date of Hearing: Tuesday 25th June 2019

Appearances: Mr J Winter (appellant) & Mrs S Harris (for the respondent
Valuation Officer)

Date of Decision: 10th July 2019

Decision of Tribunal: Appeal allowed in part

Members of the Tribunal: Mr B Fraser (Chairperson) & Mr S Hennah

Tribunal Clerk: Mr G Harris

Introduction:

1. Mr Winter contended, in a proposal to alter an entry in the 2017 Rating
List received by the Valuation Officer on 18th April 2017, that the Rateable
Value (RV) of 120 Woodville Road was incorrect and should be reduced
from £8,000 to £5,700 with effect from 1st April 2017, for the following
reason –
The property has a piece of private land (forecourt) between the front of
the shop and the pavement, yet it has been given the same rateable value
as shops nearby that don’t have this detrimental valuation feature.

2. With the agreement of both parties the tribunal consisted of two members
under Paragraph 30(2) of The Non-Domestic Rating (Alteration of Lists
and Appeals) (Wales) Regulations 2005, which states –
Where all parties to an appeal who appear so agree, the appeal may be
decided by two members of a valuation tribunal, and notwithstanding the
absence of a chairman.
3. This is a summary of the case and is not intended to be an exhaustive
record of the proceedings. However, the parties can be assured that all
the evidence was fully considered by the tribunal when it arrived at its
decision. Consequently, the absence of reference to any statement, or
evidence, should not be construed as being overlooked.

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 2 of 5
Summary of the Case

4. Mr Winter explained that he had occupied the appeal property for 10
years and expressed his shock at a 43% increase in his RV following the
revaluation in 2017. There had been no increase in rental values, and it
seemed that the VOA had just added 43% to everyone.
5. Mr Winter described Woodville Road as being the most diverse road in
the UK. Pre-war it had been the Cathays high street however following the
building of a bridge it was no longer a through road. Other areas had
prospered but Woodville Road was in decline. The opposite side of the
street had a continuous retail frontage, with a sunnier aspect and a footfall
tenfold that to his side which consisted a mixture of shops and residential
dwellings. The property next door had not been let for over 6 years and
had been converted to a house, and the property to the other side
consisted a shop with a derelict dwelling above, with the next 2 properties
along the street also being houses.
6. Mr Winter explained that the appeal property had been converted from a
house and that the forecourt area had previously been its front garden.
The local authority had insisted that a ramp had been installed on the
forecourt for disabled access to the shop in order to grant planning
permission.
7. Mr Winter stated that his main complaint was the unjustified 43% increase
in RV, considering the diversity of the street and substantial differences in
tone between the 2 sides of it. Certain ‘business’ premises in the locality
significantly reduced the tone of the area.
8. Under cross examination, Mr Winter explained that the forecourt area was
owned by the shop and that he could utilise the area to display goods if he
so wished. Mr Winter’s contention that there was tenfold increase in
footfall on the opposite side of the street had been obtained through his
own observations. Mr Winter had contended for £5,700 as this was the
RV of a property he owned on a neighbouring street which had been let to
an estate agent, a similar business to his, and which he believed to be a
fair amount.
9. Mrs Harris, for the Valuation Officer, introduced the appeal property and
provided the Tribunal with external photographs, a map of its location and
a plan of its layout together with the Valuation Officer’s survey details. It
had been entered into the 2017 Rating List at a RV of £8,000 with effect
from 1st April 2017. She explained that the basis of valuation for the
appeal property had been defined under Paragraph 2(1) Schedule 6 of
the Local Government Finance Act 1988 as –
2(1) The rateable value of a non-domestic hereditament [none of which
consists of domestic property and none of which is exempt from non-
domestic rating] shall be take to be an amount equal to the rent at which

it is estimated the hereditament might reasonably be expected to let from
year to year on these three assumptions-
(a) the first assumption is that the tenancy begins on the day by reference
to which the determination is to be made;
(b) the second assumption is that immediately before the tenancy begins
the hereditament is in a state of reasonable repair, but excluding from
this assumption any repairs which a reasonable landlord would
consider uneconomic;
(c) the third assumption is that the tenant undertakes to pay all usual
tenant’s rates and taxes and to bear the cost of the repairs and
insurance and the other expenses (if any) necessary to maintain the
hereditament in a state to command the rent mentioned above.
10. The Antecedent Valuation Date (AVD) was specified as 1st April 2015
under Paragraph 2(3)(b) of Schedule 6 of the Local Government Finance
Act 1988 as the day by reference to which the rateable value of non-
domestic hereditaments are to be determined for the purposes of the local
and central non-domestic rating lists which are to be compiled for Wales
on 1st April 2017.
11. Mrs Harris explained that the property had been inspected during January
2019 and based on the agreed revised measurements Mrs Harris had
amended her valuation. Mrs Harris’ new valuation of the appeal property

13. Mrs Harris explained that based on the rental evidence it was her opinion
that the zone A rate of £250/m2 was fair and reasonable. Accordingly, she
requested that the Tribunal confirm a RV of £7,700 with effect from 1st
April 2017.
14. Under cross examination, Mrs Harris explained that she had used the 5
comparable properties, rather than the whole street as evidence, as she
believed them to be more similar to the appeal property and were those
with rents closest to the AVD. She had not included the local Sainsburys
as a comparable property as it had been valued on a different basis being
a convenience store.
15. Mr Winter queried why Mrs Harris had not used 142 Woodville Road in
her evidence. Mrs Harris explained that she did not believe it to be
comparable as it was a newly built shop next to a residential block
separated from the appellant’s row by a side road. The Tribunal agreed to
accept 142 Woodville Road, where the rent had been analysed at
£183.92/m2 based on a total area of 142m2  with an area ITMS of
50.51m2,  as a comparable property in evidence at Mr Winter’s request.
16. At this point Mr Winter asked that the Tribunal adjourn his appeal in order
that he could gather evidence to support his contentions as he had been
unaware of what had been required prior to the hearing and had
undergone an eye operation 2 weeks previously. After considering Mr
Winter’s request the Tribunal refused the adjournment on the following
grounds –
a) Mr Winter had received a notice of hearing some 5 weeks prior to the
hearing giving the appellant sufficient time to prepare a case and
gather supporting evidence.
b) Sufficient guidance had been available from the Valuation Tribunal for
Wales should Mr Winter have requested assistance.
c) Tribunal considered that they had enough evidence from which to
make a reasoned decision.
17. At the conclusion of the hearing, the tribunal decided to reserve its
decision.

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 5 of 5
The Reasons for Decision

18. Having considered all the evidence placed before it the tribunal decided as
follows: -

19. In his proposal Mr Winter had contended that the Rating List was
inaccurate and that the RV of the appeal property should be reduced to
£5,700 with effect from 1st April 2017.

20. In cases such as this the tribunal considered that the open market rents
available on the appeal property or on comparable properties within its
locality to comprise the most compelling evidence. In the absence of
direct rental evidence on the appeal property as it was owner occupied
the tribunal examined the rents that transpired along Woodville Road. The
tribunal believed that the diversity of Woodville Road had been reflected
in the analysed rental amounts provided in Mrs Harris’ evidence which
varied from £183.92/m2 to  £389.04/m2. Looking at this rental evidence,
the tribunal deemed that the rent of the property closest in size to the
appeal property on the same side of the street and 2 doors away, 116
Woodville Road, to be a good indicator of the rental value with an
analysed rental amount of £272.62/m2.

21. The tribunal did not consider that the forecourt had detrimental effect on
the value of the appeal property as Mr Winter had initially contended for in
his proposal, as he had confirmed that it had been owned by the appeal
property and could be used for display purposes should he so wish. The
fact that he did not was irrelevant to these proceedings. The property had
also benefited from disabled access having been built upon it.

22. In light of the above, the tribunal believed that the £/m2 unit value of £250
adopted by Mrs Harris in her valuation of the appeal property was fair and
reasonable although it was at the lower end of the analysed rental
amounts of other assessments in the locality. With this in mind the tribunal
confirmed Mrs Harris’ revised assessment of £7,700.

title: 685029150022/541NV17: Maesmawr Hall, Maesmawr, Caersws, SY17 5SF
text:
Tribiwnlys Prisio Cymru

Valuation Tribunal for Wales

Appellant: Mr J Garner

Appellant’s Address: Hotel and Premises, Maesmawr Hall, Maesmawr, Caersws, SY17 5SF

The Matter Appealed against: 2017 Non-Domestic Rating List entry

Date of Hearing: 12 September 2019

Appearances: Appellant - Mr J Garner (Owner) and Mrs V Upton (General Manager) and for
the Valuation Officer (VO) - Mrs T S Davies

Date of Decision: 23 September 2019

Decision of Tribunal: Appeal Allowed in Part

Members of the Tribunal: Mr D C Subacchi (Chair), Mr W G Lewis and Mr L H Robinson

Tribunal Clerk: Mr R Williams

Introduction:

1. The subject proposal was made on the 31 May 2017 challenging the Compiled List
entry of the Hotel and Premises, Maesmawr Hall, Maesmawr, Caersws, SY17 5SF, in
the 2017 Non-Domestic Rating List at £46,750 Rateable Value (RV) with effect from
the 1 April 2017.

2. The grounds of appeal as contained in the subject proposal were as follows:

“The RV altered to maximum of 5% increase effect from 01/04/2017.

The RV was inaccurate when the property was revalued in April 2017.

Excessive increase in our small business (20 room, 3-star hotel). We are based in
Mid Wales in rural area. An increase of over £5,000 per annum is extremely difficult.”

3. At the request of Mr Garner and with the agreement of the Tribunal, the representative
for the VO presented her evidence first.

4. The following is a summary of the cases presented and is not intended to be an
exhaustive record of the proceedings. However, the parties can be assured that all the
evidence was fully considered by the Tribunal when it arrived at its decision.
Consequently, the absence of reference to any statement, or evidence, should not be
construed as being overlooked.

The VO’s Case

5. Mrs Davies reported that the basis of valuation for the appeal hereditament was
defined in paragraph 2(1) of Schedule 6 to the Local Government Finance Act 1988,
as amended by section 1(2) of The Rating (Valuation) Act.

6. She explained that the rateable value (RV) of a hereditament was an estimate of the
rental value at the Antecedent Valuation Date (AVD), which for the 2017 Non-Domestic
Rating List was the 1 April 2015, whilst having regard to the physical factors and

physical setting as they were at the Material Day, which in respect of a Compiled List
appeal was the 1 April 2017. She also confirmed that in respect of the former 2010
Non-Domestic Rating List, the AVD was the 1 April 2008 and the Material Day was the
1 April 2010.

7. The VO reported that the accepted method of valuation for licensed premises was the
profits method, which was agreed following joint discussions between the VO and
Gerald Eve, the rating adviser to the British Hospitality Association. The profits method
was considered appropriate as it was based on analysis of trading accounts and other
relevant information with the application of a rental percentage to the Fair Maintainable
Trade (FMT).

8. The FMT represents the annual trade considered to be maintainable at the 1 April
2015, having regard to the physical nature of a property and its location whilst
assuming the business will be carried out proficiently by responding to the normal
trading practices and competition of the locality. The percentages to be applied in
respect of 3 & 4 standard service hotels vary between 5.25% - 7.25%.

9. For the 2010 Rating List the adopted trade figure was £475,000 which was determined
from trade information provided. Upon receipt of trade information in respect of the
2017 Rating List, the adopted and now agreed FMT figure was £750,000. From
records provided by a colleague, she noted that an offer in reduction had been made to
£45,000 RV at a rental of 6%, reflecting the nature of the property and the ongoing
maintenance costs of a Grade II listed building. She also highlighted the fact of a
reduction of 2% in the rental bid between the lives of the 2010 & 2017 Rating Lists.

10. Mrs Davies also informed the Tribunal that Mr Garner was paying a rent of £60,000 per
annum, which suggested that the current RV of £46,750 was too low. However, the
property was occupied as a hotel and therefore due to the limited comparable evidence
available it should be valued having regard to trade. She also added that there was
also a suggestion that the passing rent was not a true open market rent as there was a
potential conflict with connected parties.

11. In conclusion whilst having regard to the type of hotel and the appeal hereditament’s
level of trade, the VO opined that the revised assessment offered to Mr Garner was fair
and reasonable. Accordingly, she requested that the Tribunal confirm a revised
assessment in respect of the appeal hereditament of £45,000 RV, with effect from 1
April 2017.

12. Following an invitation from the Chair to question the VO on the evidence she had
presented, Mr Garner declined the offer as he could not disagree with the evidence
presented. However, he commented that was unhappy with the criteria and structure
within which the VO worked under.

13. In response to questions from the Chair and the Clerk, the VO confirmed that a median
6% rental bid was applied to the appeal hereditament as it was a small 3-star country
hotel offering wedding, conference facilities with a good trade.

14. The lowest figure of 5.25% would apply to a rural ‘Travelodge’ type hotel with very
limited facilities.

The Appellant’s Case

15. Mr Garner informed the Tribunal that he purchased the Grade II listed property’s
freehold in 2008. As the property was basically in a poor state of repair and on its

knees, it required complete refurbishment and was upgraded at a massive cost.
Consequently, he applied for a commercial mortgage, a mortgage designed for
purchasing or re-mortgaging a property which was to be used as a business premises.
At present, he owes approximately a half a million pounds for the improvement costs
let alone the mortgage he still has left to pay.

16. Whilst he understands the criteria and structure within which the VO must operate, he
questioned how it was applied? At no stage had the VO requested a breakdown of his
accounts as it would detail expenses and would show that the business is not making a
profit. The VO only looks at the turnover but not the actual cost of the turnover with no
consideration for the fact that the costs of the business have gone up in line with the
turnover.

17. He explained that an element of those costs were wages and pensions. The business
employs 32 people who receive the minimum wage. However, having regard to the
nature of his business and the travelling back and forth to work, he believed it was
unreasonable to ask staff to work a minimum couple of hours and therefore he has to
employ the staff for more hours than they are actually required.

18. The appellant explained that one day the rateable value of the property was £38,000
and the next it was £46,875. In monetary terms, he was one day paying £18,000 per
annum, the next it had increased by £5,000 to £23,000 per annum. He challenged how
could the current criteria be fair when he must plan for weddings 18 months in advance
and then the VO can drop a bombshell of a 30% upsurge in costs.

19. In conclusion, Mr Garner made a plea for help in that any future notification of
increases in the rateable value was advertised more and that any such increases were
phased in over a period of time.

20. In the absence of questions, the VO commented that the draft list for the current 2017
Rating List was available to be viewed in September/October 2016 and only the
property’s rateable value would have been available to view and not the makeup of the
valuation. The draft list to the next Revaluation in 2021 will be available to view in late
2020.

21. At the conclusion of the hearing, the Tribunal decided to reserve its decision.

The Reasons for Decision

22. Having considered all the evidence placed before it, the Tribunal decided as follows:-

23. The definition of Rateable Value and the basis of valuation for the appeal
hereditament, was contained within paragraph 2 (1) of Schedule 6 to the Local
Government Finance Act 1988, as amended by Section 1(2) of the Rating (Valuation)
Act 1999.

24. The definition determines that the Rateable Value of a non-domestic hereditament
shall be taken to be an amount equal to the rent at which it is estimated the
hereditament might reasonably be expected to let from year to year, if the tenant
undertook to pay all usual tenant’s rates and taxes and to bear the cost of the repairs
and insurance and other expenses, if any, necessary to maintain the hereditament in a
state to command that rent.

25. The Tribunal was also mindful of The Rating Lists (Valuation Date)(Wales) Order 2014,
SI No.2917 (W297) which signifies that the Antecedent Valuation Date, the 1 April

2015, as the day to which Rateable Values of Non-Domestic hereditaments were to be
determined for the purpose of local and central Non-Domestic Rating Lists, compiled
for Wales on the 1 April 2017.

26. Consequently, in accordance with relevant legislation, the Tribunal must value the
appeal hereditament by reference to values pertaining at the 1 April 2015 and cannot
consider economic factors other than they were on that day; whilst having regard to the
locality that existed as at 1 April 2017.

27. The valuation method in respect of licensed premises is an accepted method that has
been agreed and which has resulted in a scheme of valuation being approved and an
appropriate guide published, based on the application of differential percentages to the
Fair Maintainable Trade and this shortened profits method has formed the primary
valuation approach for all licensed premises.

28. The Fair Maintainable Trade represents the annual trade considered to be
maintainable at the 1 April 2015, having regard to the physical nature of the property
and its location on the assumption that the business would be carried out proficiently,
by responding to the normal trading practices and competition in the locality. The
percentages to be applied would vary according to the physical characteristics of the
premises and the nature of the trade.

29. From the trading information provided, the Tribunal was persuaded that the level of
Fair Maintainable Trade agreed between the parties and adopted by the Valuation
Officer fairly reflected the trade that the hypothetical tenant would reasonably have
been expected to have achieved at the appeal hereditament at the Antecedent
Valuation Date of the 1 April 2015.

30. The Tribunal believed the evidence provided by Mr Garner was in effect a protest at
the Valuation Office Agency regarding the criteria and structure it worked within and
the implementation of taxation following revaluations. Whilst Mr Garner was entitled to
challenge the rateable value against his property by way of an appeal to the Tribunal,
any grievances in respect of the implementation of Non-Domestic Rating taxation lay
elsewhere and was not within the Tribunal’s remit.

31. Having regard to relevant legislation and considering the evidence overall, the
Members believed the Valuation Officer was correct in her assertion that the revised
assessment of £45,000 Rateable Value was fair and reasonable having regard to the
Fair Maintainable Trade of £750,000 at a rental bid of 6%.

32. In conclusion, the Tribunal allowed the appeal in part in respect of the Hotel and
Premises, Maesmawr Hall, Maesmawr, Caersws, SY17 5SF, and Ordered that the
revised assessment of £45,000 Rateable Value be entered in the 2017 Rating List, with
effect from the 1 April 2017.

is the most appropriate.  In addition, he maintained that settlement evidence

13. In relation to the Appellants’ argument concerning the rate per £m2 adopted
for 55 Bethcar Street at £86m2 and 32 Bethcar Street at £80m2, the VO
explained that these properties were both significantly larger than the
appeal property and therefore less comparable.  He clarified that the
subject property had a total area of 149m2 and ITMS 80m2; 32 Bethcar
Street had a total area of 1349.2m2 and ITMS 199.41m2 and 55 Bethcar
Street had a total area of 493m2 and ITMS 150m2.  Therefore, the

14. He also maintained that whilst 55 Bethcar Street had been valued in line
with its subject rent, that rent was further from the AVD than other rental

only and received a significant rent free period.
15. As the rents reflected those shops with standard shop frontages, the VO
stated a non-standard frontage allowance was required as the subject
property has a traditional bank frontage.  A comparable bank with a non-
standard frontage allowance of 10% was ascribed to 14/15 Market Street,
Ebbw Vale and this allowance was in line with the allowances
recommended by the Inter Banking Forum for this frontage type.  Therefore,
Mr Pearson considered a 10% frontage allowance was appropriate for the
subject property as opposed to 7.5% previously ascribed.
16. Based upon the rental and settlement evidence, the VO considered that a
rate of £105m2 was justified which resulted in a valuation of £8,500 RV.
Consequently, Mr Pearson requested that the Tribunal allow the appeal in
part and confirm £8,500 RV for 34 Bethcar Street, Ebbw Vale with effect
from the 1 April 2017.
17. In response to questions, the VO stated:
• The term ITMS stands for In Terms of Main Space.  Zone A is the
most valuable area valued at 100%, Zone B at 50% and the

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

basement as a storage area at 10%.  The toilets appear within the
valuation they are valued at £0;
• The property was measured on NIA (Net Internal Area) and in
accordance with the RICS Measuring Practice, non-structural walls
are measured through, therefore the ornate porch area was included
within the valuation;
• For the 2017 Rating List, the value per £m2 is based on annual rental
values from the AVD of 1 April 2015;
• In relation to the frontage he valued the property – ‘rebus sic
stantibus’ - as it stands and the property is currently used as a shop.
As the property does not have a typical shop frontage, Mr Pearson
considered that the previous allowance was insufficient and
increased it to 10%;
• A national rating agent did not question the £m2 attributed to 10/12

18. Mr Roberts clarified that the shop is his wife’s business and for several
years she operated a market stall throughout the Gwent area.  In the past,
the market in Ebbw Vale was very popular with limited plots available,
however nowadays you are now able to choose your plot.
19. Mrs Roberts originally rented another property, 14 Bethcar Street, but as
the rent was high she vacated this property and rented the appeal
hereditament.
20. Mr Roberts provided the Tribunal with a copy of his presentation which
included several internal and external photographs of the subject property
and a written submission, extracts of which are below:
21. Mr Roberts explained that he believed the £m2 should be reduced to
£80m2, or less, in line with 32 Bethcar Street, a shop located adjacent to
the subject property and which has the benefit of a traditional shop frontage.
This, he stated would equate to £6,400 RV.
22. In addition, the Appellant argued that as Mrs Roberts is paying a rent of
£6,000 pa to Mr Bond, the comparable RV should be circa £6,000.
23. Mr Roberts informed the Tribunal that Blaenau Gwent and Ebbw Vale is at
the top of the list for WIMD (Welsh Index of Multiple Deprivation) and has
been since this index/measure was introduced.  He explained that this has
led to any retail businesses trying to survive, not only having to deal with
the decline of bricks and mortar retail due to the popularity and ease of
online shopping, but also the economic decline of the area which
successive governments have failed to address spanning back over 40
years.

24. Mr Bond and Mr Roberts itemised other contributory factors which they felt
supported their case for a reduction in the RV ascribed to the subject
property:
25. Shop frontage – the property, a former HSBC bank, does not have the
traditional shop frontage which impacts upon attracting customers;
26. Council/Walk signage screens – one side of the property is obscured by
signage screens which block the general public viewing the one side of the
shop;
27. Market fast food outlet – during market days the one side of the shop is
obscured by a fast food outlet which has an impact on customers and
therefore trade;
28. Car parking multi storey – a multi storey car park is located at the bottom
end of the town which does not benefit businesses located at the top of the
town.  There are also problems with the lift which is regularly out of service;
29. Car parking town centre – there is limited town centre parking available and
as parking wardens now regularly patrol the area there is the increased risk
of a parking fine;
30. Since there is no back entrance to the subject property and as the Council
has marked the town centre with yellow lines, the Appellant runs the risk of
parking fines during loading/unloading goods to the appeal property;
31. Car parking at The Walk – situated opposite the subject property, The Walk
has changed ownership and is now chargeable;
32. Public transport – since 2018 Stagecoach has cut its bus services into
Ebbw Vale which has led to a decline in footfall of 60% and resulted in a
number of retail businesses struggling to survive. The Appellant had
contacted a number of organisations concerning this issue and was in the
process of running a petition;
33. Town centre regeneration – years of poor town centre planning and
refurbishment have resulted in Ebbw Vale town centre becoming a difficult
place for shoppers to visit and has resulted in a steady decline in footfall.
The Appellant had contacted his MP, AM’s and the Federation of Small
Businesses raising his concerns.  He had also found out that a number of
groups/working parties involved in regeneration have not delivered any
coherent strategy to help with the economic situation within Blaenau Gwent;
34. Public toilets - situated some 300 metres away and having only recently re-
opened, Mrs Roberts allowed visitors to the town to use the WC facilities in

35. In addition, Mr Roberts and Mr Bond were also aware that a number of

into smaller units.  Mr Bond clarified that he has been offering shops at £50
per week but there has been no uptake.
37. To conclude, Mr Roberts reiterated that the appeal property does not lend
itself to a retail premises as the windows are high and narrow.
38. In response to questions, Mr Bond and Mr Roberts stated:
• As owner, Mr Bond does not want the ornamental porch area in the
property removed as it is very decorative and in-keeping with the
property.  Mr Roberts stated that the double doors also help with
keeping the heat in.  They did initially use this area to display goods
but these were stolen.
39. Both parties were given the opportunity to summarise their cases:
40. Mr Pearson informed the Tribunal that he had fully considered the
Appellants arguments.  The subject property had been re-measured and
he had considered a basket of rents and settlements from Bethcar Street
which supported £105m2 being ascribed.  In addition, he had taken into
account the non-traditional frontage and increased the allowance from
7.5% to 10% in line with a similar allowance ascribed to a comparable bank
in Market Street.  Any physical changes to the locality after the 1 April 2017,
the compilation date of the 2017 Rating List, would need to be addressed
by submitting a further proposal to the VOA.  He requested that the Tribunal
confirm a revised RV of £8,500 with effect from the 1 April 2017.
41. Mr Roberts thanked the Tribunal for listening to his case and explained that
he strongly believes that town centres should be re-generated as they form
part of a community.  He requested confirmation of £80m2 in line with other
properties within Bethcar Street.  Whilst he appreciated that the rent
payable may sound low, it is the amount that town centre traders can afford.
42. Mr Bond stated that he did not consider that non-domestic rates should be
payable whilst a property is being renovated.
43. At this point, Mr Pearson clarified that when a property is being renovated,
the taxpayer can approach the VOA to establish whether that property is
capable of beneficial occupation.

44. At the conclusion of the hearing, the Tribunal decided to reserve its decision.

Reasons for Decision

45. Having considered all the evidence placed before it the Tribunal decided as
follows:

46. In his proposal Mr Bond contended that the Rating List was inaccurate and
that the appeal property’s assessment should be reduced from £12,250 RV
to £8,000 RV with effect from the 1st April 2017.  However, at the hearing,

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 9 of 10
the Appellants considered that the RV should be reduced to circa £6,000
RV in line with the rent that Mr and Mrs Roberts are paying Mr Bond.

47. Mr Bond also maintained that the classification as a bank and premises
should be changed to a shop and premises, which the VO had agreed to
prior to the hearing.

48. Therefore, the only issue in dispute for the Tribunal to consider was the price
per m2 as applied by the VO to the property.  The VO had considered the
Appellants’ contentions and agreed that a reduction in the £m2 was
warranted from £140m2 to £105m2 and the non-standard frontage
allowance should be increased from 7.5% to 10% which equated to a
revised Rateable Value of £8,500 effective from the 1 April 2017.

49. However, the Appellants argued that the property should be valued in line
with larger shops located within close proximity to the subject property, 55
Bethcar Street at £85m2 and 32 Bethcar Street at £80m2.  They also
referred to a number of issues which they stated currently blight Ebbw Vale
town centre.

50. The Tribunal was aware that in accordance with relevant legislation the
appeal hereditament must be valued by having regard to values achieved
as at the Antecedent Valuation Date, the 1 April 2015, whilst looking at the
physical circumstances of the property as at the Material Day, the Compiled
List entry date of the 1 April 2017.

51. Whilst the Tribunal appreciated the current issues concerning Ebbw Vale
Town Centre as conveyed by Mr Bond and Mr Roberts, in relation to the
subject appeal it cannot have regard to any issues that have occurred after
the 1 April 2017.  The Members are aware that physical changes within a
locality may have an impact on the RV of a property and a proposal for a
reduction
in
assessment
because
of
a
“material

of
circumstances”(MCC) can submitted to the VOA in accordance with the
Non Domestic Rates  (Alteration of Lists and Appeals)(Wales) Regulations
2005 SI 758(W.63).  However, the issue of an MCC fell outside of the scope
of this particular appeal.

52. In accordance with principles outlined in Lotus and Delta v Culverwell (VO)
& Leicester City Council the rental evidence on the appeal property should
be taken as a starting point for the RV. However, the Tribunal was mindful
that the passing rent was effective from the 1 February 2018, nearly three
years after the Antecedent Valuation Date, and had no defined tenure or
terms.  Accordingly, the Tribunal attached little weight to this evidence.

53. The Tribunal considered a basket of rents and settlements from similarly
sized shops, ITMS, located on Bethcar Street in order to establish the
hypothetical rent for the appeal property as at the 1 April 2015.

54. The Members noted that the closest new letting to the AVD occurred on the
20 May 2014.  54 Bethcar Street, a traditional shop amongst a parade

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 10 of 10
situated further along Bethcar Street, analysed to £110.09m2.  The VO
adopted £100m2.

55. Some two weeks later on the 1 June 2014, a further new letting was agreed
on another traditional shop and premises, 41 Bethcar Street.  This rent
analysed at £105.54m2 with the VO having adopted £160m2.

56. In addition, a rent review was agreed on 10/12 Bethcar Street, a bank and
premises with shop frontage, on the 20 August 2015, just under five months
after the AVD.  This rent analysed at £107.58m2.  It was noted that an
appeal submitted by a national firm of rating agents, CBRE, agreed a 10%
allowance for layout and frontage but the rate of £160m2 was not challenged
thereby appearing to suggest that the agent did not consider it to be
excessive.

57. With relation to those properties cited as comparable by the Appellants
namely, 55 Bethcar Street and 32 Bethcar Street, the Members agreed with
the VO that these properties were considerably larger than the subject
property, and as such, were not as comparable as the smaller properties
within Bethcar Street.

58. Therefore, whilst the Members sympathised with the Appellants regarding
the issues they raised concerning the current retail climate in Ebbw Vale,
from the evidence provided, they did not consider that the revised rate of
£105m2  proposed by the VO was excessive as it appeared to be in line
with other similar properties within Bethcar Street.

59. Consequently, in view of the above, the Tribunal determined that the
£105m2 adopted by Mr Pearson in his valuation of the appeal property was
fair and reasonable. With this in mind, the Tribunal confirmed the VO’s
revised assessment of £8,500 RV  with effect from the 1 April 2017 for Shop
and Premises 34 Bethcar Street, Ebbw Vale NP23 6HQ and allowed the
appeal in part.

4. This is a summary of the case and is not intended to be an exhaustive

5. As is customary in cases of this nature where the proposal challenged the
Valuation Officer’s Notice, Mrs Harris was invited to present the Valuation

6. In her opening statement, Mrs Harris pointed out that she represented the
Valuation Officer for Wales in a dual role of advocate and expert witness.

7. In her role as advocate, Mrs Harris explained how the proposal came to be
made and, with reference to its Parts B (details of the Proposed List
Alteration) and C (Grounds for your proposed alteration), she set out the
parameters and scope of the issues that were under appeal.

8. Mrs Harris then referred to Paragraph 2 (1), Schedule 6 of the Local

The rateable value of a non-domestic hereditament … shall be taken to

property despite the fact that it was situated at the other end of Newgale

Page 8 of 10
number of well-known retail outlets such as Greggs, Specsavers and a

which might only be in existence for another six years and which suffered
from numerous closures during the winter. The area was supported by a
population of approximately 43 people. He added that the only viable
businesses in the area were those in the tourism industry. He referred to
conclusions drawn by Mr Parr on the same matter who opined that the
property would be hard to let at a value above £7,500. He said that the
uncertainty of the area’s continued existence would militate against
anyone starting a business in the area. He did not accept that the 2017
level of value should be greater than that of the 2010 level of value and
sought a value of RV £8,500 with effect from 1st April 2017.

34. At the conclusion of the hearing, the Tribunal decided to reserve its
decision.

Decision of the Tribunal

35. Having considered all of the evidence placed before it, the tribunal decided
to allow the appeal but only to the extent Mrs Harris conceded in her
valuation.

36. In making its decision, the Tribunal was mindful of Schedule 6 of the Local
Government Finance Act 1988, as amended which defined Rateable Value
and to which Mrs Harris spoke to in her advocate’s evidence.  As a
consequence of this, the Tribunal understood that in the context of a rating
valuation one had to consider and determine what rent the appeal property
could reasonably have been expected to realise had it been let on the open
market as at the 1 April 2015 - that being the antecedent valuation date for
the purposes of all entries in the 2017 Rating List. The Tribunal was also
required to bear in mind the statutory assumption one must make regarding
the terMrs of the presumed letting and the date at which various, mainly
physical factors relevant to the property and its locality, must be considered.
In this case the day on which physical matters must be contemplated (the
‘material day’) was 1st April 2017.

37. The judgment in Lotus and Delta Ltd which Mrs Harris advanced in her
evidence, provided guidance on the weight to be attached to rental and
assessment evidence.  This case also maintained that one would consider
the rent on the subject property as the correct starting point in such an
exercise. In addition, it was held that the passing rents on similar
properties could be examined where they were available as were the
assessments on comparable properties.

38. The Tribunal considered that the 1st December 2017 rent on the appeal
property was tainted as a result of an in-house connected party
arrangement and therefore carried no weight. Moreover, it transpired some
two and a half years from the AVD and this did little to inform the Tribunal

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 9 of 10
as to how reflective it was of open market values that prevailed at that
time. As a consequence, the Tribunal was not convinced by the appellant’s
rationale for using a rent such as this in these proceedings.

39. The Tribunal was not persuaded that the November 2014 rent of Sands
Café should be regarded as unrealistic as Mr Carter had described it in his
evidence. The reason for this was because the rental value for this
property was  struck between unconnected parties some 5 months prior to
the AVD. The Tribunal did not consider the fact that the property was
subsequently sold in 2015 invalidated the usefulness of this piece of
evidence.

40. The Tribunal attached little weight to the evidence contained in Mr Parr’s
February 2017 letter because it related to an earlier appeal that Mr Carter
had made in respect of the appeal property’s 2010 Rating List valuation.
Mr Carter had not persuaded the Tribunal that the relevance of particulars
of properties situated elsewhere in Haverfordwest and its environs and
cited in this schedule of evidence bore any relevance to the issues now
under consideration.

41. The Tribunal observed that Sands café and Pebbles at Chapel Farm had
certain physical characteristics that were arguably superior to those at
Newgale House. Both comparable properties benefitted from larger
windows, car park and beach side access. However, the Tribunal had
noted during the cross-examination of evidence, that Sands enjoyed an A3
class of use which the Tribunal deduced may have made the property
more desirable. Moreover, the appeal property’s underlying level of value
of £55/m2 was considerably lower than these properties and, in the
absence of more compelling evidence, it was difficult for the Tribunal to
conclude that the Valuation Officer’s revised valuation of the subject
property was unreasonable.

42. Mr Carter contended that owing to ecological factors, commercial viability
in Newgale could only be sustained for a finite period of time. The Tribunal
understood that the local authority had made proposals about how to
manage the effects of the sea on Newgale but apart from some
exploratory works which were undertaken after the 2017 list came into
force, nothing physical had taken place in the area. With this in mind, one
had to take account of the physical nature of the appeal property and of
the area in which it was situated on the material day, which in this case
was 1st April 2017. Should the area be subject to a future material change
in circuMrstances then such matters could be reflected in a separate
proposal, but this appeal could not reflect circuMrstances that had yet to
take place.

43. The Tribunal appreciated Mr Carter’s obvious frustration that several
different caseworkers had been assigned to this case. However, this was
not a matter that fell into the Tribunal’s jurisdiction, nor did it feel that
comments about this would be appropriate to make within the scope of this
appeal.

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 10 of 10

44. Although the Tribunal understood that Mr Sanderson remained concerned
with the level of value he had agreed with the Valuation Officer in respect
of Sands Café and Newsurf, there was no avenue, for the reasons Mrs
Harris spoke to in her case, for redress here. Even if the motivation for him
saying this was to assist the appellant in his case, such comments were
without foundation and therefore attracted  little weight.

45. Whilst the Tribunal accepted that the circuMrstances at Newgale were
unique, one must also reflect on the fact that this area is renown as an
area of outstanding natural beauty as well as highly regarded by water
sport/leisure enthusiasts. Mr Carter maintained the view of his appointed
representative that no one would pay more than £7,500 per annum in rent,
yet the Tribunal had observed that the operator of Sands Café had done
precisely that only a matter of months prior to the AVD. There was no
evidence before the Tribunal which suggested that if vacant and to let at
the AVD, the appeal property being significantly larger property would
command a rent less than that actually achieved for Sands Café.  Mr
Carter suggested the underlying level should be half that proposed by the
Valuation Officer. However, he had not, in the Tribunal’s opinion produced
evidence of sufficient strength that supported that contention. As a
corollary, the Tribunal was not prepared to revise the compiled list entry
beyond that conceded by the Valuation Officer in this case.

46. The parties are entitled to appeal to the Upper Chamber of the Lands
Tribunal within 28 days of the date of this decision. In making its decision,
the Tribunal orders the Valuation Officer to amend the 2017 Rating List to
accord with this decision.

allowance should be given. With reference to appeals which were made by
the ratepayers of neighbouring properties and following an inspection of
the area on 22nd March, the VO concluded that the works that affected the
properties in this location subsisted for approximately 13 weeks.

25. The roadworks completely closed the road junction and some pavements
around Church Street, Cresswell Street and St Georges Street from 2nd
January. The road outside properties in this vicinity were dug up by
Western Power up to 9th February 2018. After this, Pembrokeshire County
Council re-laid the whole surface moving along St George’s Street towards
Lower Frog Street and The Arches. The works consisted of two contiguous
schemes and were directly outside the property for approximately 13
weeks. The bulk of the work was completed in the third week of March
2018. Some work was re-done and machines were parked outside the
appeal property whilst the works moved up the road towards Lower Frog
Street. With reference to photographs taken on 22nd March 2018, Mrs
Harris pointed out that the works had been completed at that point.
Another photograph taken on the same day depicted the works moving
along St George Street and away from the appeal property.

26. Mrs Harris said that a rent of £25,000 pa was paid on the property and that
the landlord had not offered the tenant a concession during the duration of
the works. However, she reminded the Tribunal that the VO must assume
a hypothetical situation in which a reasonable landlord would be prepared
to accept part of any loss rather than lose a tenant. In such a scenario the
hypothetical landlord would reduce the rent in order to reflect the
disturbance caused by roadworks.

27. With reference to her Appendix 2; these contained details of the
appellant’s trade for the period 7th January 2018 to 25th March 2018 which,
if compared with the corresponding period in 2017, showed that trade had
diminished by some 9.45%. Mrs Harris said that if  one accepted that the
landlord might be prepared to accept part of any loss, she estimated a
reduction in RV would equate to 5%. However, the VO had to give a
considered view of the impact of disruption to all affected occupiers rather
than to just the appellant ratepayer by virtue of the use she had put to the
premises. In the case under consideration, Mrs Harris proposed an end
allowance, which was accepted by other neighbouring ratepayers, of 10%.

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 6 of 8

28. Since the nature of the road works was temporary, Mrs Harris asked the
Tribunal to make an order in under Regulation 34 (6) of the Non-Domestic
Rating (Alteration of Lists and Appeals) (Wales) Regulations 2005, as
amended. In this regulation stated –

Where it appears that circumstances giving rise to an alteration
ordered by a valuation tribunal have at the date of the decision ceased
to exist, the order may require the alteration to be made in respect of
such period as appears to the tribunal to be commensurate with the
duration of those circumstances.

29. In light of this Mrs Harris asked the Tribunal to confirm a revised list entry
of RV £16,000 with effect from 2nd January 2018 until 1st April 2018.

30. At the conclusion of the evidence the Tribunal decided to reserve its
decision.

Decision of the Tribunal

31. Having considered all of the evidence placed before it, the Tribunal
decided to allow the appeal to the extent Mrs Harris had conceded in her
evidence. The reasons for this were set out as follows -

32. When arriving at its decision, the Tribunal was governed by the rating
legislation laid down by Parliament.  Section 1(2) of the Rating (Valuation)
Act 1999 which amends paragraph 2(1) of Schedule 6 of The Local
Government Finance Act 1988 required that the rateable value of a
property is the amount that the hypothetical tenant coming fresh to the
scene would pay in rent on an annual basis assuming that the tenancy
began on the material day and that the property was put into reasonable
repair prior to the tenancy beginning, excluding any repairs that the
hypothetical landlord would consider uneconomic.  It is assumed that the
tenancy would have a reasonable prospect of continuance and that the
tenant would be responsible for all repairs and insuring the property.
Moreover, in rating, all hereditaments must be assumed to be vacant and
available to let on the statutory terms of the hypothetical tenancy.

33. The property and its locality must be considered as they physically existed
at the material day but at the level of rental values and in the economic
climate that existed as at the antecedent valuation date (AVD).  The AVD
was set by the Rating Lists (Valuation Date) (Wales) Order 2014  –

1st April 2015 is specified as the day by reference to which the rateable
values of nondomestic hereditaments are to be determined for the
purposes of local and central non-domestic rating lists which are
compiled for Wales on 1st April 2017.

34. The scope of this proposal only addressed the disruption caused by
roadworks situated within the vicinity of the subject property for the period

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 7 of 8
2nd January 2018 to 1st April 2018. The scope of the proposal could not be
extended to consider matters that subsequently occurred later in the year.
Whilst Mrs Harris had accepted that the road works had lasted long
enough and were sufficiently severe that the hypothetical landlord would
accept a lower annual rent, the question the Tribunal had to address was
had the appellant justified a further reduction beyond that conceded by
Mrs Harris in her revised valuation.

35. The Tribunal found nothing inherently wrong with Mrs Harris’ process
which involved looking at the scheme of works, considering its duration
and severity and, with reference to other forms of evidence such as the
previous year’s trade for the corresponding period, deduced that an end
allowance of 10% was fair and reasonable. This level of end allowance
was offered to and accepted by other occupiers in the vicinity, irrespective
as to whether they traded or not. The fact that a company did not trade
during the works did not mean that traders who did gained more of an end
allowance. Whilst the Tribunal also appreciated that trade gained from
regular customers might be lost, it considered that the reduction offered in
Mrs Harris’ valuation adequately reflected the temporary loss in trade.
There could be no compensation to reflect lost custom per se or to reflect
the time for that trade to return.

36. The Tribunal did not consider that the council’s failure to remove plant and
machinery away from the street at weekends added to the appellant’s
contention for a further reduction in her property’s RV. If the local authority
had promised to move equipment on the weekends but did not, then
redress for this, if there was any, lay elsewhere.

37. Whilst the Tribunal understood that works prevailed throughout parts of the
town, it was evident from the photographs supplied by Mrs Harris that
there were no works outside the appeal property by 22nd March. The
photographs showed that the works had gradually progressed along St
Georges Street towards the junction with Lower Frog Street.

38. The Tribunal attached no weight to the fact that a different end allowance
was given for a longer period in respect of disruption caused to business in
2012- 13. The appeal under consideration was made against an entry in
the 2017 Rating List whereas the issues referred to by Mrs Uka above
reflected circumstances which occurred during the life of the 2010 list.

39. The Tribunal noted that this case had been adjourned from a hearing
scheduled earlier in 2019 and understood Mrs Uka’s frustration of having
to attend a subsequent hearing at her own expense. However, the
Tribunal was not empowered to award costs to a party either by way of
compensation or in the event of their success at the hearing.

40. In its conclusion, the Tribunal did not believe that Mrs Uka’s case for a
reduction beyond that offered by Mrs Harris was justified for the reasons
given above. As a corollary, the Tribunal found by the facts presented that
the appeal property’s Rateable Value should be reduced to £16,0000 with

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 8 of 8
effect from 2nd January 2018 until 1st April 2018 and orders the Valuation
Officer for Wales to alter the Rating List to accord with its decision.

Introduction:

1. Mr Dyke-Price made a proposal to alter an entry in the 2017 Non-
Domestic Rating List in relation to the appeal hereditament, shop and
premises, 48-50 High Street, Rhyl.  The Valuation Officer (VO) received
the proposal on 20 April 2018 and in making his proposal, the appellant
sought a reduction in the appeal hereditament’s entry in the Rating List
from £50,000 to £28,000 with effect from the 1 April 2017.

2. The following is a summary of the case and is not intended to be an
exhaustive record of the proceedings. However, the parties can be
assured that all the evidence was fully considered by the Tribunal when it
arrived at its decision. Consequently, the absence of reference to any
statement, or evidence, should not be construed as being overlooked.

Summary of the Appellant’s Case

3. Mr Dyke-Price confirmed that as things had moved on since he had
submitted the appeal proposal, he could no longer support his original
valuation of £28,000 Rateable Value (RV).  He was now asking the
Tribunal to consider reducing the RV to £15,250 per annum.
4. He contended that over the last 8 to10 years, the impact of on-line
shopping, the opening of Parc Prestatyn and other off-centre retail units
had resulted in the increase of empty units in Rhyl town centre.  During

Non-Domestic Rating Decision
