this time, new occupiers mainly consisted of charity shops, discounters
and temporary trades, all on heavily incentivised terms, which negated the
concept of open market rental evidence.
5. Mr Dyke-Price stated that over the last 8 to 10 years there were no
retailers who would trade across two floors in Rhyl.  He believed for the
appeal hereditament to have been let in April 2015, consideration would
have had to be given to voiding the second floor and part of the first.
6. The appellant told the Tribunal that a passing rent of £80,000 p.a. was
agreed in January 1993, which had no relevance to the rental value as at
the 1 April 2015, some 22 years later.  The lease was for 25 years and
despite an upwards only rent review, the rent was never increased.  He
noted also that tenants such as Marks & Spencer, Next, Top Shop,
Mothercare, Dixons, Clarks, Goldsmiths, Evans ladies wear and JJB
Sport were all in the town centre at the time and all had vacated.
7. He stated that since 2008/10 the market for global rents of £30,000 -
£50,000 p.a. did not exist for High Street units in towns such as Rhyl.  The
trend had been away from larger units.  He argued that no tenant would
have leased a property of 637.35 sq.m in the centre of Rhyl High Street at
a rent above £15,000 p.a. in April 2015.
8. In order to factually support this view, Mr Dyke-Price stated that 37 High
Street, Rhyl was let in March 2013 to W.H. Smith at a Zone A value of
£103 and was re-let again in July 2017 at the same rental.  This factor
underlined the tone of the list for a property of this size (344 sq.m).
However, the appeal property was 85% larger at 6,858 sq. ft.  Mr Dyke-
Price could not see how the appeal property would attract a higher rental
value per sq. ft. than W.H. Smiths.
9. The appellant told the Tribunal that the VO had recently agreed the Rating
tone of the list with Paul Coope of GL Hearn Ltd, acting for the Rating
Surveyor’s Association (RSA), at £200 Zone A.  The tone of the list
essentially determines what a hypothetical standard unit in a certain
location would let for in the open market.  A standard unit was 18’ x 60’
with the same cover at the first floor.  The appeal property was 3 times the
size of a standard unit and to arbitrarily apply a percentage discount to
reflect size did not bear any relation to the reality of the marketplace.  In
the market since 2010/12, it was sadly an assessment of how low you
have to go to find a tenant and not take the tone of the list and apply a 15,
25, 50 or 75% discount to result in the correct market rent or indeed a
letting.  Mr Dyke-Price argued that whilst tone of list generally worked for
standard units, it failed when it came to one-offs which in his opinion
should be considered in isolation because of their advantages or in this
case disabilities.
10. Mr Dyke-Price addressed the VO’s 15% discount for size that had also
been applied in Wrexham. He argued that applying or relying on
percentages to prove a rental was pointless and it was rather what a
particular property would let for in the open market at a certain point in

time.  Arcadia trading as Burtons and Dorothy Perkins had offered nil rent
to stay in the appeal property with rolling breaks of 4 months.  This
demonstrated their view of the unit’s likely profitability and the
marketplace generally.  The property had been on the market since
January 2017 to sell or let and no rental offers had been received
whatsoever.
11. Mr Dyke-Price drew the Tribunal’s attention to 56 High Street, Rhyl which
was a few doors from the appeal property and half its size.  This property

since.  He said that it was the rental judgement he disputed and the fact
that the market for units of this size in towns such as Rhyl was non-

£103 Zone A.  He explained that he had accepted the VO’s areas but

17. Mr Wynn-Cowell explained that a reduction to £200 Zone A for this part of
the High Street had been agreed following extensive discussions between
the VOA and the Rating Surveyor’s Association (RSA) represented by Mr
Paul Coope of GL Hearn.  He stated that three appeals on High Street
Rhyl, which were listed on this Tribunal, had been agreed based on a
£200 Zone A figure.
18. Mr Wynn-Cowell said that the appellant may frame the dispute in a
different way to the VO, nevertheless he was arguing that the dispute can
be seen to turn on the quantum of the percentage discount for the size of
the shop.  He submitted that the increase to 15%, from the historic 4%
was fair and reasonable.
19. In similar circumstances appeal 30660055 was recently agreed with North
Block Ltd at 23/24 Hope Street, Wrexham where a 15% discount for size
was agreed.
20. In conclusion of his evidence Mr Wynn-Cowell stated that at the
Antecedent Valuation Date (1 April 2015) the passing rent between
Arcadia and the landlord was £80,000.  Arcadia vacated the property at
the end of their lease in 2017.  He understood that the rent was increased
to £80,000 at a rent review in January 2003 and remained unchanged
until the termination of the lease (25 Years from Dec 1992).  No weight
had been attached to this rent.
21. At the conclusion of the hearing, the Tribunal decided to reserve its
decision.

The Reasons for Decision

22. Having considered all the evidence placed before it, the Tribunal decided
to dismiss the appeal.  In arriving at its decision, the Tribunal gave the
following reasons.

23. It made its decision having regard to the prevailing legislation: Schedule 6
of the Local Government Finance Act 1988.

24. Mr Dyke-Price had contended that the Rating List was inaccurate and that
the RV for the appeal property should be reduced to £15,250. In cases
such as this higher court authorities had accepted that the burden of proof
rested with the appellant on the basis that ‘he who asserts must prove.’
Moreover, it was an accepted tenet of law that any assertions made
before a Tribunal should be underpinned by evidence. Therefore, in the
case under consideration the persuasive burden of proof rested with the
appellant ratepayer and not the respondent Valuation Officer by virtue of a
statutory duty to prepare and maintain the Rating List.

25. The Tribunal believed the appellant had not been able to sustain his
argument that the assessment was incorrect and had not, with reference
to evidence, undermined the Valuation Officer’s valuation of the property.
The Tribunal believed that Mr Wynn-Cowell had correctly valued the

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 6 of 6
property taking into account the whole shop area, on the assumption that
the hereditament was empty and to let.  Under the same assumption the
Tribunal saw no reason to disregard the second floor as contended for by
Mr Dyke-Price.

26. The Tribunal accepted that the unit value of £200 for Zone A used by Mr
Wynn-Cowell in his valuation of the property was in line with the
settlement evidence agreed between the VOA and the agent of the
ratepayers located on the High Street in Rhyl.  The unit’s size had been
reflected in the 15%allowance and the resulting revised assessment of
£28,750 was fair and reasonable.

27. Although the Tribunal was sympathetic to the plight of the appellant and
appreciated the tough trading conditions faced in the area, it did not
believe that any hard evidence had been provided to justify such a
reduction in the property’s rateable value.

28. With this in mind, the Tribunal decided to allow the appeal but only to the
extent conceded by Mr Wynn-Cowell in his valuation. As such, the
Tribunal orders the Valuation Officer to amend the Rating List with its
decision.

TRIBIWNLYS PRISIO CYMRU
VALUATION TRIBUNAL FOR WALES

Appellant: Poundland Limited

Appeal Address: Shop and Premises, The Co-Operative Food, Berriew Road,
Welshpool, SY21 7SN

The Matter Appealed against: 2017 Non-Domestic Rating List

Date of Hearing: 2 October 2019

Appearances: Mr G Garnett of Colliers International (Appellant) and Mrs C M
Jones representing the Valuation Officer (VO)

Date of Decision: 19 November 2019

Decision of Tribunal: Appeal Allowed

Members of the Tribunal: Mr R J Higginson (Chair), Mr J R Pyrke and Mr R S
Smith

Tribunal Clerk: Mr R Williams

Introduction:

1. The subject appeal arose from a proposal submitted by Colliers International on
behalf of Poundland Limited on the 6 July 2018 challenging the Compiled List
entry of the Shop and Premises, The Co-Operative Food, Berriew Road,
Welshpool, SY21 7SN, in the 2017 Non-Domestic Rating List at £82,000
Rateable Value (RV) with effect from the 1 April 2017.

2. The grounds of appeal as contained in the proposal were: “The Rateable Value
altered to £1 with effect from 01-Apr-17. The entry in the Rating List is incorrect,
unfair, excessive and bad in law and should be reduced to £1. Effective Date:
01 April 2017.”

3. The following is a summary of the case and is not intended to be an exhaustive
record of the proceedings. However, the parties can be assured that all the
evidence was fully considered by the Tribunal when it arrived at its decision.
Consequently, the absence of reference to any statement, or evidence, should
not be construed as being overlooked.

Agent’s Case

4. Having introduced himself and submitted copies of his presentation to the
Tribunal, Mr Garnett clarified that the photographs contained therein served to
illustrate the condition of the appeal hereditament as at 9 July 2015 and that the
trade information included should be ignored.

2

5. He reported that the issue of dispute between the parties was the RV applied to
the appeal hereditament and he contended that it should be reduced to £30,000
RV with effect from 1 April 2017.

6. The appellant referred to the basis of valuation as defined in paragraph 2(1) of
Schedule 6 to the Local Government Finance Act 1988, as amended by section
1(2) of The Rating (Valuation) Act 1999, which provided the definition of RV of a
non-domestic hereditament and the assumptions to be made. He explained that
the RV of a hereditament was an estimate of the rental value at the Antecedent
Valuation Date (AVD), which for the 2017 Non-Domestic Rating List was the 1
April 2015, whilst having regard to the physical factors and physical setting as
they were at the Material Day, the 1 April 2017.

7. Mr Garnett reported that the appeal hereditament was entered in the 2017
Rating List at £82,000 RV which he considered excessive having regard to the
propositions set out in case law in respect of Lotus and Delta v Culverwell (VO)
and Leicester CC (1976) which established that when arriving at an opinion of
RV, the rent should be taken as the starting point, and O’Brien v Harwood
(2003) which set out the three stages leading to the establishment of a tone of
the list, whilst the physical characteristics of the property should be considered
in accordance with W H Smith & Son v Clee (VO) (1978) and Kotecha v
McKillop (VO) (2014), and the Valuation Office Agency’s 2017 Valuation Scales.

8. He also referred to the Court of Appeal decision in respect Ladies Hosiery and
Underwear Ltd v West Middlesex Assessment Committee (1932) which set out
the principle that valuation should be a means of establishing the correctness of
the assessment rather than uniformity.

9. In support of his contention that the appeal hereditament’s RV was excessive,
the appellant informed the Tribunal that the subject property was a dated food
store extending to 1,371m2, located in the market town of Welshpool, in a non-
tourist agricultural area with a population of approximately 7,000 people.

10. Mr Garnett clarified that on the 21 March 2011, Tesco opened a new purpose-
built superstore of 4,595m2, which as a result changed retail shopping on offer
in Welshpool, which already had a Sainsburys, a Morrisons superstore and a
good selection of other shops. As a result, the Co-Operative could no longer
trade viably from the subject property and consequently ceased trading in
September 2012.

11. Following the Co-Operative’s closure, the appeal hereditament was marketed
and let to Poundland at the following rents:

• 17/08/15 - 16/08/16 £1
• 17/08/16 - 16/08/17 £1
• 17/08/17 -  onwards £31,000

12. He opined that the rental evidence was of the highest order and that it also
emphasised that no other major retailer wanted the appeal hereditament; Lidl
did not want to occupy and Aldi built a bigger “limpet store” of 1,741m2 near the

3

Tesco store in 2017. Consequently, Poundland occupied the subject property at
a price.

13. Having regard to the House of Lords decision in Robinson Bros (Brewers) v
Durham County Assessment Committee (1938), he opined that the rent passing
on the property was ‘prima facie’ the best evidence. However, the rent needed
to be adjusted for the two years at £1 and the third year at £31,000 along with
the fact that there had been a recession post 2008 and he questioned whether
this area of Wales had come out of the recession? He did however accept to
some extent that the recessionary impact could be ignored as Tesco was built
in 2011 and Aldi in 2017.

14. The appellant commented that the VO would suggest that the passing rent was
not a clean rent. He however contended that the rental evidence was of the
highest order and fell into line with the definition of RV as contained within the
1988 Act.

15. Mr Garnett pointed out that whilst the appeal hereditament had repair issues in
the past, the subject property was not derelict as suggested by the VO and
referred to the photographic evidence of the appeal hereditament’s condition as
at 9 July 2015. He confirmed that whilst he had not personally surveyed the
subject property, as a surveyor when considering the photographic evidence, he
estimated that the repair figure would have been in the region of £10,000.

16. Following enquiries and as being the long lessee, the Co-Operative opined that
the cost of repair was in the region of £30,000. He also enquired with
Poundland as to how much was actually spent and despite numerous requests,
Poundland could not provide the requisite information. However, his client
confirmed that £29,546 was spent on ventilation and electrics and therefore he
could only assume that the Co-Operative had put the property into repair.

17. The appellant then referred to the lease acquisition schedule drawn up between
surveyors and solicitors on behalf of the landlord, Wesleyan Assurance
Society, and the tenant, Poundland, dated 8 January 2016, which was a sub-
lease of the lease agreed on 8 March 1988 between the landlord and the former
tenant, Somerfield Stores Limited. Despite every effort, he had been unable to
acquire a copy of the original lease. He referred to the following details from the
sub-lease:

• no capital contribution;
• no works to be undertaken by the tenant;
• a rent of £1 per annum with effect from 17 August 2015, exclusive of VAT,
with no rent-free period, expiring on the 16 August 2016;
• security of tenure outside the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954;
• the tenant whilst being allowed to sell anything had a wide usage of the
property; and
• a full repair insuring lease with the tenant keeping the property in good
condition excluding repair to the roof and lift which was the landlord’s
responsibility.

4

18. Mr Garnett pointed out that the legal definition of RV dictated it was the tenant’s
responsibility for repair and not the landlord’s, however the sub-lease detailed
that repairs to the roof and lift were the responsibility of the landlord.
Consequently, he assumed that the rent would be higher if the landlord took
responsibly for such repairs.

19. He then referred to the renewal lease agreed on 22 September 2017 at £31,000
per annum with effect from 17 August 2017, which was agreed very close to the
Material Day of 1 April 2017, and contained the following details:

• security of tenure outside the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954 indicating that at
the end of the lease the landlord does not have to allow the tenant to
continue with occupation and therefore the tenant had no security of tenure;
• a break clause on or after 17 April 2018; and
• the roof and lift being excluded from the tenant’s repair liability.

20. The appellant queried that as the tenant had no security of tenure outside the
1954 Act, would the condition effect value? He opined that it would if it were a
different property in a better location however not in respect of the subject
property as it was difficult to let. He had enquired with colleagues experienced
in such matters whom suggested that the difference in value, if any, could
possibly be in the region of circa 5-10%.

21. Mr Garnett contended that having regard to his practical experience in valuing
shops both within the Valuation Office Agency and private practice, he had no
choice other than to make an educated guess in carrying out a valuation on the
‘back of a fag packet’ in that that the subject property’s assessment should be
£30,000 RV based on the fact that the store was dated in design, the retail area
had low headroom with no retail frontage to the High Street and did not have its
own car park only the local authority car park that was never free. He also
pointed out that loading to the store was difficult as trucks had to drive into the
adjacent public car park to reverse into the loading bay, which proved difficult
even on a quiet Sunday lunchtime. The main street would ‘snarl up’ with the
least amount of traffic.

22. He also pointed out that appeal hereditament was empty for several years
before his client occupied the subject property at a price.

23. In the appellant’s opinion Welshpool was a quiet depressed small Welsh town
whereas Shrewsbury to the east was the main centre of population and public
resort with Newtown to the west a more important centre locally. The main
source of employment in Welshpool was agriculture and there was little or no
tourism in the immediate locality and therefore it was a low value socio
economic area.

24. Mr Garnett pointed out that as at the Material Day of 1 April 2017, Welshpool
had the following retailers located within the town and was effectively ‘over
shopped’:

5

• a modern Morrisons superstore with a large free car park and good
access/egress;
• a good compact Sainsburys with its own car park and two road access
points, one being onto an ‘A’ road;
• a good new Tesco superstore with its own car park in an excellent location;
and
• a selection of local independent shops.

25. He contended that the best evidence was that of the new letting of Poundland,
which represented the hypothetical tenant coming fresh to the scene.
Poundland was given two years rent free and then the third year at £31,000 per
annum. He questioned how to deal with two years rent free along with an
expenditure of £29,546 and suggested it was effectively a trade off with the
capital sum equating to almost a year’s rent. He also commented that whilst one
year rent free was outside the formal lease, as at the AVD, the rent passing on
the appeal hereditament was a £1.

26. The appellant reminded the Tribunal of the proposition given in  Lotus and Delta
v Leicester City Council and Culverwell (VO) which established the hierarchy of
evidence and that nothing supersedes a letting to a hypothetical tenant coming
fresh to the scene.

27. He challenged how any competent experienced valuer could ignore the rental
evidence passing on the appeal hereditament at the 1 April 2015 whilst having
regard to competition and its letting history, reminding that discount retailers
such as Aldi, Lidl and Wilko did not want the subject property however
Poundland occupied the property at a price.

28. In conclusion, Mr Garnett requested that the Tribunal reduce the appeal
hereditament’s assessment to £30,000 RV with effect from 1 April 2017.

29. During cross examination, the appellant reiterated that both the Co-Operative
and his client Poundland could not provide him with the requisite information.
He could only assume that the Co-Operative carried out some repair work as
the property was vacant before his client occupied. Poundland confirmed that
£29,546 was spent on ventilation, electrics and some plumbing works, which he
opined was effectively one year rent free.

30. He did not agree that the majority of leases were covered by the Landlord and
Tenant Act (1954) and suggested that it would depend on the type of property.

31. He did not believe that the repair review exclusion from the Landlord and
Tenant Act (1954) would have made a difference as both parties agreed to an
early break clause.

32. He opined that the market for large shops between 2015 – 2017 would have
been weak having regard to some depressed areas of Wales and as a
consequence location would have had an influence on the rental market
suggesting that a good shop in the right location would rent and conversely, a
poor shop in a bad location would not.

6

33. He also confirmed that the rent of £31,000 was an on-going rolling rent based
on an understanding between the parties where the landlord wanted the
property occupied and the tenant was happy to continue.

34. The other repairs carried outside the figure of £29,546 spent by Poundland
would have been in the majority ‘minor issues’, as shown in the photographs
dated 9 July 2015, and in his experience the repair cost would have been in the
region of £10,000.

35. His valuation of £30,000 RV was based on an overall basis and not a price per
meter squared.

Valuation Officer’s Case

36. Having introduced herself to the Tribunal, Mrs Jones reiterated that the issue of
dispute between the parties was the appeal hereditament’s compiled list
assessment and that she would be seeking confirmation of a reduced
assessment of £47,750 RV, with effect from 1 April 2017.

37. She referred to the basis of valuation as defined in paragraph 2(1) of Schedule
6 to the Local Government Finance Act 1988, as amended by section 1(2) of
The Rating (Valuation) Act 1999, and explained that the RV of a hereditament
was an estimate of the rental value at the AVD, which for the 2017 Non-
Domestic Rating List was the 1 April 2015, whilst having regard to the physical
factors and physical setting as it was as at the Material Day, the 1 April 2017.

38. The VO referred to the principles regarding hierarchy of evidence established in
Lotus and Delta v Culverwell (VO) and Leicester CC (1976) and the direction
given in the case of O’Brien v Harwood (2003) regarding the establishment of
tone of the list.

39. Mrs Jones reported that the appeal hereditament occupied a town centre
position opposite Morrisons and had a large local authority car park to the rear.
It was built approximately 1985 and had a total area of 1371.15m2 over the
ground and first floors.

40. Referring to the case of Lotus & Delta, she intimated that the starting point was
to look at the rent passing on the property itself and that the more closely the
circumstances under which the rent was agreed, both as to time, subject matter
and conditions, relate to the statutory requirements, the more weight should be
attached to it.

41. The VO reported the rents passing on the appeal hereditament:

• £1 August 2015 until August 2016 – sublet from Co-Op to Poundland;
• £1 August 2016 until August 2017 – sublet from Co-Op to Poundland;
• £31,000 August 2017 until August 2018 – let from Wesleyan Assurance to
Poundland;
• £31,000 August 2018 for 3 years.

7

42. Mrs Jones had sought clarification of several issues regarding the rent from Mr
Garnett, however he could not provide any further details. She had also
requested copies of the leases but to no avail.

43. Regarding the issue of repair, she reported that Mr Garnett stated in his
evidence that she had contended the appeal hereditament was derelict. As an
explanation, she clarified that she had discovered an online article stating that
the subject property was derelict which prompted her to query with him via e-
mail as to “what sort of state was the building in” and “did Poundland have to do
any works to the property”. The appellant confirmed that the property was not
derelict however it required some works.

44. The VO contended that those works were required to be taken into account
when considering the rent and RV. The definition of Rateable Value states that
before the tenancy commences, the property was assumed to be in a
reasonable state of repair. Mr Garnett provided a report in December 2015
regarding a schedule of dilapidation works quoting a total cost of £33,679 for
repairs, which included £18,783 for external repairs. He also provided details
that Poundland had spent £29,546 on repairs when it occupied the appeal
hereditament in respect of electrics, ventilation and flooring with no mention of
any external repairs. She questioned that had the subject property required
£18,783 to be spent on external issues to return it into a reasonable state of
repair, should not that amount be factored in when adjusting the rent along with
the repair costs spent by Poundland. Having regard to this information she
suggested that a figure of almost £50,000 worth of work would need to be
factored in when adjusting and analysing the rent.

45. Mrs Jones then referred to issues regarding the leases explaining that the first
two leases were sublets from the Co-Operative to Poundland and the third was
from Wesleyan Assurance to Poundland. The Co-Operative’s lease was to
continue until 2022 however despite requesting clarification from Mr Garnett
regarding as to what happened with the Co-Operative’s lease, the sublets and
the new lease, no information or answers had been provided in the continuing
absence of copies of the leases.

46. She opined that when the Co-Operative agreed to sub-let to Poundland, it was
assumed that the Co-Operative was in discussions regarding surrendering the
lease. As a consequence, the prospect of continuing the lease would have been
limited, as it may have been unclear to Poundland whether they would have
been able to agree a new lease with the head landlord once the Co-Operative
had vacated, which as a consequence would have affected the rent that
Poundland would have been prepared to pay.

47. The VO added that as the first two leases were between the Co-Operative and
Poundland and the third between Wesleyan Assurance and Poundland, they
should not be looked at together as they were with different landlords and
therefore should be considered separately. The third lease was from August
2017, two years after the AVD when the market for large shops fell over this
period and therefore a rent considered two years post AVD was not ideal.

8

48. Mrs Jones pointed out that a major issue with the rents was that the leases
were contracted out of the Landlord and Tenant Act (1954). She explained that
the 1954 Act gave tenants the right to renew their lease at the end of a tenancy
on broadly similar terms. Having regard to personal experience she opined that
being contracted out of the 1954 Act meant that the tenant had no right to
renew the lease, which would have been of benefit to the landlord and therefore
was likely to affect how much rent would be agreed. Consequently, the tenant
was more likely to pay below market rent as it would have had no security of
tenure. She had asked Mr Garnett for clarification as to why these leases were
contracted out but to no avail.

49. She reminded the Tribunal of the definition of RV which states that “the rent at
which it is estimated the hereditament might reasonably be expected to let from
year to year”. She commented that if the tenant has no security of tenure then
the rent does not comply with the definition of RV.

50. The VO referred to the principles established in Lotus & Delta in that “the more
closely the circumstances under which the rent agreed both as to time, subject
matter and conditions relate to the statutory requirements contained in the
definition of gross value….the more weight should be attached to it”. She
concurred that the rent was a starting point and given all the issues concerning
repairs, being contracted out of the Landlord and Tenant Act (1954), two
different landlords, lease surrender issues and the third lease being two years
post AVD in a falling market, it was clear that the rent did not comply with the
statutory definition of RV. Therefore, it was difficult to attach much weight to the
rent albeit it provided a guide as to a minimum value.

51. Mrs Jones referred to her comparable properties of other large shops situated in
Welshpool and Newtown as follows:

• The Old Station Yard, Welshpool, SY21 7AY - 834.60m2 - £80,000 RV – No
IPP, Non-Zoned, £105/m2.
• 35-36 Broad Street, Welshpool, SY21 7RR – 984.60m2 - £46,000 RV – No
IPP, Zoned at £265/m2.
• National Westminster Bank, Broad Street, Welshpool, SY21 7RP –
270.76m2 - £36,500 RV – No IPP, Zoned at £265/m2
• 16/17 Broad Street, Welshpool, SY21 7SD – 431.63m2 - £33,250 RV – No
IPP, Zoned at £265/m2
• Charlies Stores, Market Street, Newtown, SY16 2PD – 1162.52m2 - £72,500
RV – No IPP, Zoned at £180/m2
• Argos, Wesley Street, Newtown, SY16 2NH – 840.37m2 - £77,500 RV – No
IPP, Zoned at £325/m2.

52. Having considered the rent and the comparable assessment evidence
available, she opined that Mr Garnett’s valuation at £30,000 RV was too low as
it sat out of line with other assessments.

53. In summary, Mrs Jones reminded the Tribunal that the leases were contracted
out of the Landlord and Tenant Act (1954). Consequently, the tenants had no
security of tenure and therefore would have been prepared to pay less rent. The

9

tenant would also have been required to put the appeal hereditament into a
reasonable state of repair and therefore the repair costs needed to be factored
in, which would result in the rent being higher. Also due to the likelihood of a
lease surrender there would have been reservations in the mind of the tenant as
to whether it could continue with its occupation when the sublet had ceased.
Likewise, the third lease was two years post AVD in a falling market and
although the rent was a starting point, it was of limited assistance albeit it gave
an indication as to a minimum level of value.

54. In conclusion, the VO requested the Tribunal confirm a reduced assessment of
£47,750 RV, with effect from 1 April 2017.

55. Responding to questions from Mr Garnett, Mrs Jones confirmed that in the
absence of the lease and an agreement between the parties, she had no option
other than to assume that the rent was low due to the lack of security of tenure.

56. In respect of her comparable assessments she verified that she had not
inspected the properties. She accepted the appellant’s contention that no
appeals had been made against those assessments and his observations in
respect of The Old Station Yard, Welshpool, that it was a former converted
railway station built in 1870, occupied by the retailers Edinburgh Woollen Mill
which catered mainly for tourists. Unlike the appeal hereditament it benefited
from its own car park and was located on the main by-pass road to Welshpool.
It was a completely different type of property to the appeal hereditament and
was not valued by zoning.

57. She confirmed that 35-36 Broad Street, Welshpool, was valued by zoning
however it was irrelevant who occupied and when it was built. She also verified
that the property at the National Westminster Bank, Broad Street, Welshpool,
was a former bank that was valued as a retail premises.

58. In view of the VO’s responses, Mr Garnett suggested that her comparable
properties were not similar on a like for like basis to the appeal hereditament
and that Newtown was not comparable to Welshpool, as Newtown was a larger
town. Accordingly, he recommended that the VO’s comparable properties be
disregarded.

59. At the conclusion of the hearing, the Tribunal decided to reserve its decision.

60. Note not forming part of the decision. Clerical errors were identified in the
appellant’s submission – Point 7 the Valuation Office Agency’s Valuation Scales
should read 2017 and not 2010, and at Point 11, the commencement date for
the first year at a rent of £1 should read 17 August 2015 not 7 August 2015.

The Reasons for Decision

61. Having regard to relevant legislation, the referenced case law and the evidence
provided, the Tribunal decided as follows:

10

62. The Tribunal was mindful that Non-Domestic property must be valued in line
with the statutory definition of Rateable Value, as contained in paragraph 2(1) of
Schedule 6 of the Local Government Finance Act 1988, as amended by Section
1(2) of the Rating (Valuation) Act 1999, and in accordance with The Rating Lists
(Valuation Date)(Wales) Order 2007, Statutory Instrument No: 2007/3153
(W269), which determined that the appeal hereditament must be valued by
having regard to rental values achieved at the Antecedent Valuation Date, 1
April 2015, whilst looking at the physical circumstances of the property at the
Material Day, 1 April 2017.

63. It was also aware that the appeal hereditament must be assumed to be “vacant
and to let” and cannot have regard to the actual trade of the occupier and that it
was important to ascertain whether a tone of value had been established.

64. Referring to the statutory definition of Rateable Value and the Lands Tribunal
judgement in Lotus & Delta v Culverwell (VO) and Leicester City Council (1976),
the Tribunal was mindful that the best evidence was provided by rents
synonymous with the statutory definition, passing on the subject property and
which required little or no adjustment.

65. The Tribunal was also conscious of the High Court case of Vines Ltd v De
Mauny (VO) (2010) which provided guidance that it was for the appellant to
demonstrate that the existing assessment was incorrect and not for the
Valuation Officer to prove that it was right. However, the case of Oldschool &
Oldschool v Coll (VO) (1995) offered guidance in that the Valuation Officer was
required to provide comprehensive, impartial evidence to achieve correct
assessments and not simply to win rating appeals.

66. Therefore in respect of the subject appeal, the Tribunal’s determination simply
fell either in favour of the appellant, who referred to the rent passing on the
appeal hereditament in support of his contention for a reduced assessment of
£30,000 RV, or the Valuation Officer, who had regard to the passing rent as an
indication to the minimum level of value along with cited comparable
assessments of large shops within Welshpool and Newtown in support of a
revised assessment of £47,750 RV.

67. It was unfortunate that the agent had been unable to provide a copy of the lease
agreed between Wesleyan Assurance Society and the Co-Operative. However,
in absence of that lease, the Tribunal could only assume that the repairs were
carried out under the sub-letting between the Co-Operative and Poundland,
which would have been amortised over the length of that lease, which was
effectively £1 per annum for two years. However, the Tribunal attached little
weight to that rental evidence as it appeared that the Co-Operative wanted to
avoid paying empty property rates for the period concerned, where it was tied
into the head lease, and consequently was attempting to surrender it.

68. However, the Tribunal was persuaded by the appellant that the passing rent of
£31,000 agreed in September 2017 should be utilised, as the rent was
reasonably clean apart from the tenant’s lack of security of tenure and the
landlord’s retention of responsibility for repair to the roof and lift. In the absence

11

of any other comparable rental information to the contrary, the Tribunal attached
greater weight to the rent agreed between the landlord and tenant passing on
the appeal hereditament.

69. This was also supported by the history in respect of the appeal hereditament
where prior to Poundland occupying in August 2015, the subject property had
been empty for over 3 years since the Co-Operative vacated in September
2012, which highlighted the disadvantages associated with the appeal
hereditament i.e. dated design, low retail area headroom, no retail frontage to
the High Street, no dedicated parking and poor loading/unloading facilities.

70. Whilst the Members appreciated that the lease lacked the opportunity for the
tenant to automatically renew, it was agreed for a term of 3 years and case law
has stated that the definition of RV requires a rent on an annual basis with a
reasonable prospect of continuance.

71. It was also noted that numerous major retail stores were present in Welshpool,
and at that time, none were interested in occupying the appeal hereditament
other than for Poundland, who sub-let the subject property from the Co-
Operative in August 2015 for two consecutive years at £1 before negotiating a
new lease with the landlord, Wesleyan Assurance Society, at £31,000 in
September 2017.

72. The Tribunal attached limited weight to the comparable properties relied upon
by the Valuation Officer, as they were either town centre retail type units within
Welshpool, other than The Old Station Yard which was a former converted
railway station, or were located in the different town of Newtown. The Tribunal
was also conscious that the Valuation Officer had not inspected the properties
and therefore was not aware of each comparable property’s character or
location.

73. The Valuation Officer was seeking a reduction in the original complied list
assessment from £82,000 RV to £47,750 RV based on the assumption that
there was a downturn in shop rental values between 2015 and 2017; however,
no evidence was provided to support this contention.

74. Accordingly, the Tribunal allow the appeal as contended by the appellant and
confirm that the entry in the 2017 Non-Domestic Rating List in respect of the
Shop and Premises, The Co-Operative Food, Berriew Road, Welshpool, SY21
7SN, be amended to £30,000 Rateable Value with effect from 1 April 2017.

Certified a true copy on 18 November 2019
property: The Co-Operative Food, Berriew Road, Welshpool, SY21 7SN

text:
TRIBIWNLYS PRISIO CYMRU - VALUATION TRIBUNAL FOR WALES

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 1 of 3

Appellant: Mr Harminder Sandhu

Appeal Property: Queens Fish and Chips, Unit 4 Stradey District Centre,
Maesycoed, Stradey SA15 4EB

Appeal number: 682930948457/192NV17/10

The Matter Appealed Against: 2017 Rating List

Date of Hearing: 16th May 2019

Appearances: Mr M Dolben (for the respondent Valuation Officer)

Date of Decision: 24th May 2019

Decision of Tribunal: Appeal allowed in part

Members of the Tribunal: Mr H Pattrick (Chairperson), Mr JG Edwards & Mr
JM Griffiths

Tribunal Clerk: Mr G Harris

Introduction:

1. The appeal under consideration followed a proposal made by Mr Sandhu
in respect of Queens Fish and Chips, Unit 4 Stradey District Centre,
Maesycoed, Stradey which the respondent Valuation Officer received on
14th September 2018. The proposal sought a reduction of the Rateable
Value (RV) of the appeal property from £14,000 to £4,200 on the grounds
that –
Currently the payable annual rent is £10,500 so the rating of £14,000
should be sufficiently lower. I am aware larger similar premises are paying
in the region of £4,200.

2. This is a summary of the case and is not intended to be an exhaustive
record of the proceedings. However, the parties can be assured that all
the evidence was fully considered by the tribunal when it arrived at its
decision. Consequently, the absence of reference to any statement, or
evidence, should not be construed as being overlooked.

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 2 of 3
Summary of the Case

3. Mr Sandhu was unable to attend the hearing and requested that the
appeal be heard in his absence. As such, the Clerk read out Mr Sandhu’s
written submission before the panel which stated –

I apologise I was unable to attend the hearing today but wish to submit a
written submission for consideration. Our current rateable value is
£14,000 which I believe is too high and wish to appeal because of the
following reasons:
1. Our neighbour unit (Co-Op, Unit 1 Stradey District Centre, Maesycoed,
Stradey, Llanelli SA15 4EB) is being charged £100 per m2/unit
whereas my much smaller unit is being charged £150 per m2/unit.
Based on their much higher turnover this I would deem unfair.
2. The other units along our parade are currently closed and not trading
so the footfall in the area is much smaller and a contributing factor to
the hardship we are currently facing.
3. I believe the flat rate which has been calculated for our unit is for the
whole site and not just the retail area. The unit is split into a traditional
fish and chip shop take away so there is a small customer waiting
area, then serving area with the majority of our unit floor space being
dedicated to our kitchen/food preparation area.
4. Our current rent is £833.33 per month so annually this is
approximately £10,500
I urge you to review our appeal and reduce the rate.
4. Mr Dolben introduced the appeal property and provided the Tribunal with
external photographs and a map of its location. He explained that it
originally been valued in line with Dominos and Subway, both located in
the centre of Llanelli, adopting a unit value of £150/m2.  This had been
supported by the Form of Return (FOR) rent given as £14,322.24 with a
6-month rent free period, the landlord responsible for external repairs and
£5,250 paid to secure the lease.
5. Mr Dolben stated that the appellant had clarified that the subject property
was not located within the town centre of Llanelli but on a primarily
residential street in the district of Stradey. In addition, the FOR rent had
mistakenly included a management charge and insurance. The actual rent
figure was £10,000 with a 6-month rent free period, with the landlord
responsible for external repairs and £5,250 paid to secure the lease. The
adjusted rent was £10,714 per annum which adjusted to £114.47/m2.
6. Mr Dolben explained that he considered the subject rent to be the best
evidence in line with the Upper Tribunal case Lotus and Delta. He had
adopted a unit value of £115.00/m2, and proposed the following revised
valuation -

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 3 of 3

7. Mr Dolben did not believe Mr Sandhu’s comparison between the appeal
property and the Co-operative located next door to be helpful as the
appeal property was much smaller, 93.6m2 compared to 342.88m2. In
addition, the subject property had been valued as a restaurant/food unit
and the Co-operative as a convenience store.
8. In conclusion, it was Mr Dolben’s opinion that the current tone adopted
was incorrect and having regard to the evidence he requested that the
Valuation Tribunal confirm a revised rateable vale of £10,750 with effect
from 11th May 2018.
9. At the conclusion of the hearing, the tribunal decided to reserve its
decision.

The Reasons for Decision

10. Having considered all the evidence placed before it the tribunal decided
as follows: -

11. In his proposal Mr Sanhu had contended that the Rating List was
inaccurate and that his RV should be reduced to £4,200. In cases such as
this higher court authorities had accepted that the burden of proof rested
with the appellant on the basis that ‘he who asserts must prove.’
Moreover, it was an accepted tenet of law that any assertions made
before a Tribunal should be underpinned by evidence. Therefore, in the
case under consideration the persuasive burden of proof rested with the
appellant ratepayer and not the respondent Valuation Officer by virtue of a
statutory duty to prepare and maintain the Rating List.

12. The Tribunal was of the opinion that the appellant had not been able to
sustain his argument that the assessment was incorrect and had not, with
reference to evidence, undermined the Valuation Officer’s valuation of the
property. The Tribunal believed that Mr Dolben had correctly valued the
property on an overall basis, considering the whole floor area on the
assumption that the property was empty and to let, and had not restricted
his valuation to the retail area as contended for by Mr Sandhu.

13. The Tribunal accepted that the unit value of £115/m2 used by Mr Dolben
in his valuation of the property was in line with the adjusted rent, and that
the resulting revised assessment of £10,750 was fair and reasonable.

14. With this in mind, the Tribunal decided to allow the appeal but only to the
extent conceded by Mr Dolben in his valuation. As such, the tribunal
orders the Valuation Officer to amend the Rating List with its decision.

text:
TRIBIWNLYS PRISIO CYMRU  -  VALUATION TRIBUNAL FOR WALES

Council Tax Liability Appeal

Page 1 of 5

Appellant: Mr M Pye

Appeal Property Address: 26 Timber Hill, Haroldston, Broad Haven, SA62
3LZ

Appeal number: 6845M8/CTL

The Matter Appealed against: BA decision to introduce a Second Home
Premium on the appeal property with effect from 1st April 2017

Date of Hearing: 9th May 2019

Appearances: Mr J Jones (for respondent Billing Authority – Pembrokeshire
County Council)

Date of Decision:

Decision of Tribunal Panel:  Dismissed

Members of the Tribunal: Mr D O Evans (Chairperson), Mr J G Edwards &
Mr J O Peake

Tribunal/Panel Clerk: Mr J Evans

Summary of the case

1. This appeal came to the Valuation Tribunal for Wales under s.16 of the
Local Government Finance Act 1992, as amended because
Pembrokeshire County Council (PCC), refused to remove a second home
premium it had imposed on the appeal property 26 Timber Hill,
Haroldston, Broad Haven.
2. This is a summary of the case and is not intended to be an exhaustive
record of the proceedings. However, the parties can be assured that all
the evidence was fully considered by the panel when it arrived at its
decision. Consequently, the absence of reference to any statement, or
evidence, should not be construed as being overlooked.
3. Mr Pye was unable to attend the hearing but asked that his case, which
was submitted to the panel by way of a written submission, was dealt with
in his absence.
4. On 27th September 2018, PCC wrote to Mr Pye and told him that it would
not remove the second home premium it had applied to the appeal
property. In its reasons for this, PCC explained that a Class 6 exemption
for seasonal homes did not apply to chalets at Timber Hill holiday park.

COUNCIL TAX DECISION

Page 2 of 5
5. Mr Pye appealed PCC’s decision to the Valuation Tribunal for Wales on
11th October 2018 and is the matter now before a panel of the Valuation
Tribunal.
6. With reference to paragraph 41 of the exemption guidance notes, Mr Pye
explained that Class 6 included purpose-built holiday homes or chalets
which were subject to planning conditions that restricted all year-round
occupancy. He explained that Timber Hill was a purpose-built chalet park
and that his chalet had never been used for year-round residency. He
added that that year-round occupancy at the chalets was prohibited and
sales between interested parties were conveyed on that understanding.
Moreover, the site was closed for November, January and February and
chalets could not be occupied during those periods.
7. Mr Pye said that paragraph 41 of the PCC’s guidance notes made it clear
that the Class 6 exemption was created with chalets in mind although it
had some discretion in how council tax charges were levied.
8. Timber Hill holiday park is an on-site local family business who own
approximately half the chalets. The other chalets were privately owned
and pay an annul fee to the site owners. The council tax premium had
motivated some of the private owners to rent out their chalets which
entitled them to business rate relief. This created direct competition with
the holiday park business. Mr Pye said that the unintended consequence
of the 50% premium was to reduce council tax income from chalet
owner’s holiday and redirect that income to the private chalet owners. Mr
Pye said that he had considered such an undertaking in order to cover
increased costs. He added that the only way to be sure of the “70 day”
rental rule is to undercut the rents charged by the site owner so that we
take business that would have otherwise gone to the holiday business
park.
9. No incentive exists for prospective holiday home purchasers to buy a
holiday chalet in Timber Hill. Mr Pye explained that a better option might
be for one to buy a property in the village or town and pay the 50%
council tax premium and avoid paying site fees whilst acquiring a more
substantial asset. He said that this worked against the aims of the second
home charge.
10. In closing statement, Mr Pye said that purchasers at Timber Hill were not
restricting the availability of homes for local people or pushing up house
prices or causing potential homes to be left empty. The premium made it
harder for one to sell chalets when other chalet parks in Pembrokeshire
where the premium did not apply. This disadvantaged chalet owners and
the holiday park business and did not help local tourism.
11. Mr Pye said that he had been happy to pay 100% council tax in order to
support local services. However, he believed that the 50% second home
premium at Timber Hill was not  within the spirit of the premium policy. In
view of the foregoing, Mr Pye asked the panel to grant an exemption from
the second home premium.

COUNCIL TAX DECISION

Page 3 of 5
12. In his evidence for PCC, Mr Jones confirmed that the issue under
consideration related to the council’s decision not to award a class of
exemption to the appeal property.
13. Mr Jones said that as a result of an error that went back to 1993, during
the planning process a three-month restriction was not placed on the
property. However, the lease agreement for the chalets stipulated that the
chalets could not be occupied for the months November, January and
February. Unfortunately, this error was not corrected.
14. On 10th March 2016, PCC resolved to introduce the second home
premium with effect from 1st April 2017.
15. Under Section 12B of the Housing (Wales) Act a billing authority may
determine that properties that are empty for long periods (second homes)
may, provided certain criteria are met, be subject to increase the
chargeable amount by no more that 100%. In order that such an increase
can apply the property concerned must have no resident and be
substantially furnished.
16. Whilst Mr Jones accepted that certain classes of property were exempted
from the higher amount under the Council Tax (Exceptions to Higher
Amounts) (Wales) Regulations 2015, he pointed out that the appeal
property did not fall within the qualifying criteria for Class 6 because the
occupation was not restricted by a planning condition.

17. In support of his case, Mr Jones referred to the s.12 of the Housing
(Wales) Act 2014 – s.12B Higher amounts for dwellings occupied
periodically: Wales and to the Council Tax (Exceptions to Higher
Amounts) (Wales) Regulations 2015 – s.12B Dwellings occupied
periodically – Class 6. Mr Jones also included a redacted copy of a
decision the Valuation Tribunal for Wales which was issued in April 2017
in respect of another property situated at Timber Hill in which the same
matter currently before the panel was rehearsed.

18. In summary, Mr Jones said that chalet 26 did not fall within the jurisdiction
of Class 6 because its occupation was not restricted by a planning
condition as defined by the regulations. He added that in this case, the
planning condition referred to any condition imposed on planning
permission granted or deemed to have been granted under Part 3 of the
Town and County Planning Act 1990.

19. In view of the foregoing, Mr Jones asked the panel to dismiss the appeal.

20. At the conclusion of the hearing the panel decided to reserve its decision.

COUNCIL TAX DECISION

Page 4 of 5

Decision of the Panel

21. Having considered all the evidence placed before it and of the statutory
provisions which Mr Jones had advanced in his evidence, the panel
decided to dismiss the appeal. In arriving at its decision, the panel gave
the following reasons.

22. Under Section 12B of the Housing (Wales) Act 2014 which provided the
definition of “second home”.  The definition of “second home” was set out
as follows –

12B Higher amount for dwellings occupied periodically: Wales

(1)For any financial year, a billing authority in Wales may by
determination provide in relation to its area that if on any day the
conditions mentioned in subsection (2) are satisfied in respect of a
dwelling –

(a)  the discount under section 11(2)(a) does not apply, and

(b)  the amount of Council tax payable in respect of that
dwelling and that day is increased by such percentage of
not more than 100 as it may specify in the determination.

(2)The conditions are –

(a) there is no resident of the dwelling, and

(b) the dwelling is substantially furnished.

23. The panel recognised that Mr Pye had acknowledged the chalets could
not be used nor were they ever used for all year-round occupancy.
However, in its reading of S.12B of the Act, the panel could not see how
Chalet 26 could have avoided the second home premium. Whilst it
accepted certain political or financial considerations altered the dynamic
of how chalets on Timber Hill were occupied and used, the fact remained
that with regard to the appeal property and its nature, there was no
resident at the property and there was no evidence to show it was not
substantially furnished.

24. The definition of Class 6 Exception was contained in The Council Tax
(Exceptions to Higher Amounts) (Wales) Regulations 2015. The class of
dwellings prescribed for the purpose of this regulation (“Class 6”)
comprises every dwelling the occupation of which is restricted by a
planning condition preventing occupancy for a continuous period of at
least 28 days in any one-year period.

COUNCIL TAX DECISION

Page 5 of 5

25. The substance behind PCC’s decision not to except the subject property
from the premium under Class 6 of the Council Tax (Exceptions to Higher
Amounts) (Wales) Regulations 2015 was grounded in the fact that the
restrictions placed on occupancy of Timber Hill in November, January and
February did not come about as a result of a restrictive planning condition
that would have been granted under the Town and County Planning Act
1990. The condition for Class 6 is met if occupation of a property was
restricted by a planning condition which prevents occupation of a
continuous period of 28 days. Since the restriction to occupy Chalet 26
was stipulated in the lease rather that of planning control, it was clear that
the statutory condition for Class 6 was not met.

26. The panel noted Mr Jones’ remarks that this lapse in planning control had
not been corrected since it was first discovered in 1993. It was evident
that redress, if there was any, associated with planning matters at Timber
Hill fell within the jurisdiction of the planning authority since such matters
fell outside the remit of the billing authority.

27. In view of the foregoing, the panel considered that PCC was correct to
apply the second home premium. Since the appeal property did not fall
within the definition prescribed for Class 6, it also saw no basis upon
which it could apply the exception Mr Pye had sought in his appeal and
dismissed the appeal.

TRIBIWNLYS PRISIO CYMRU - VALUATION TRIBUNAL FOR WALES

COUNCIL TAX DECISION

Page 1 of 6

Appellant: Mr C Bedford

Appeal Number:  6835M11/CTL/1

Appellant’s Address: 5, Alpha Chapel, Greenfield Road, Holywell CH8 7QB

The Matter Appealed against:  Council Tax Liability Appeal

Date of Hearing: 4 April 2019

Appearances:  Mr C Bedford
Mrs V Hankin Flintshire County Council (FCC)

Date of Decision:    20 May 2019

Decision of Tribunal: Appeal Dismissed

Members of the Tribunal:
Miss M Jones

Mrs J Caldwell

Mr G Hutchinson

Tribunal Clerk: Mrs C Jones

Introduction:

1. The appellant appealed against FCC refusal to grant him a Class J
exemption.  He was also aggrieved that; FCC had charged him a 50%
premium on 5 Alpha Chapel because it considered that it was his second
home for the period 1 May 2018 to 24 September 2018.

2. This is a summary of the case and is not intended to be an exhaustive
record of the proceedings. However, the parties can be assured all the
evidence was fully considered by the tribunal when it arrived at its
decision. Consequently, the absence of reference to any statement, or
evidence, should not be construed as being overlooked.

Summary of the Billing Authority’s Evidence

3. Mrs Hankin on behalf of FCC distributed her evidence pack to the Tribunal
which contained the following: -

• Skeleton Argument
o Factual Background
o Legal Framework & Issues
• Appendix 1 -   Council Tax Change of Address form
completed by appellant submitted 1 May 2018
• Appendix 2 -   Demand Notice issued to appellant 3 May 2018
showing award of Single Person Discount (SPD)

COUNCIL TAX DECISION

Page 2 of 6
• Appendix 3 -    Email from appellant on 5 July 2018 applying for
Class J exemption
• Appendix 4 -   Email to appellant on 25 July 2018 informing

him he did not qualify for the Class J exemption as

5 Alpha Chapel was not his sole or main residence
(SOMR)
• Appendix 5 -   Council Tax (Exempt Dwellings) Order 1992
• Appendix 6 -   Email reply from the appellant on 25 July 2018
disagreeing with refusal to grant Class J, felt that under
section 4 he did qualify
• Appendix 7 -   Email from appellant 15 August 2018
stating his car insurance, bank docs. etc were
addressed to him at his father’s address 141 Saughall
Road, Chester
• Appendix 8 -   Email reply to appellant 15 August 2018
clarifying the legislation regarding Class J exemption
• Appendix 9 -   Email from appellant 15 August 2018
with proof of car insurance & bank statement being
registered at father’s address in Chester
• Appendix 10 - Diary note of telephone conversation with
appellant 16 August 2018
• Appendix 11 - Email sent to appellant 25 September 2018 notifying of
final decision
• Appendix 12 - Revised demand notice (25 September 2018)
• Appendix 13 - Diary note of telephone conversation with
appellant 25 September 2018
• Appendix 14 - Email from appellant 25 September 2018 stating he was
moving into 5 Alpha Chapel as his sole or main
residence
• Appendix 15 - SPD awarded to appellant new demand notice issued
30 January 2019
• Appendix 16 - Part 7 Housing (Wales) act 2014

4. Mrs Hankin explained that on the 1 May 2018 the appellant notified FCC
that he had moved into the appeal property which was a rented property.
The appellant was awarded an SPD from that date and a demand notice
was issued on 3 May 2108.

5. On the 5 July 2018 the appellant contacted FCC by telephone having
received a final notice for non-payment of council tax.  He informed FCC
that he had not received the demand notice or the reminder because he
was a live-in carer for his father in Chester.  He rented the property when
he was on holiday from his work and was under the impression, he didn’t
have to pay council tax because of his job.  The appellant was asked to
confirm this in writing for FCC to review his account.

6. Mrs Hankin stated that FCC received an email from the appellant on the 5
July 2018 stating he wished to apply for an exemption from paying council
tax as he was a live-in career for most of the year in Chester and the

COUNCIL TAX DECISION

Page 3 of 6
appeal property was left unoccupied.  FCC replied by email on the 25 July
2018 informing the appellant he didn’t qualify for Class J exemption
(dwellings left empty by people providing care because 5 Alpha Chapel
was not his SOMR when he left to provide care.

7. The appellant replied on the 25 July 2018 stating he used the appeal
property as a base to stay during holidays, illness and other emergencies.
He believed under Section 4 he qualified for the exemption.  This was
followed by another email from him on the 15 August 2018 stating his car
insurance and other documents were addressed to him at his father’s
address in Chester.

8. On the 15 August 2018 FCC responded to explain that the legislation
stated that the exemption could only be granted on an unoccupied building
that was previously the SOMR of a person who had moved out and had
his/her SOMR elsewhere to provide care.  Mrs Hankin stated that due to
the fact the appellant had only recently moved to 5 Alpha Chapel, it couldn’t
be classed as being his SOMR before he moved in with his father.

9. Mrs Hankin explained that the appellant further emailed FCC on the 15
August 2018 with proof of his car insurance and his bank statement being
registered at his father’s address in Chester.  Due to receiving this
information FCC spoke to the appellant on the 16 August 2018 to clarify
whether 5 Alpha Chapel was in fact his SOMR.

10. The appellant’s council tax account was reviewed, and a decision made on
the 25 September 2018 that 5 Alpha Chapel was the appellant’s second
home and his SOMR was with his father in Chester.  The appellant was
advised of this and a revised demand notice was issued to him including a
50% council tax premium.  Mrs Hankin stated that FCC had the authority to
charge a 50% premium on all long-term empty properties and second
homes.  He was also advised of the reasons for not awarding the Class J
exemption and directed to the Valuation Tribunal if he wished to appeal this
decision.

11. On the 25 September 2018 FCC received an email from the appellant
stating he would be moving into 5 Alpha Chapel as he couldn’t afford to pay
the premium and would hand in his notice caring for his father.  He also
stated that when the tenancy at 5 Alpha Chapel expires on the 1 May 2019
he would be moving out of the property and had informed his landlord of
this.

12. Between October 2018 and January 2019 FCC were in correspondence
with the appellant regarding him providing evidence he had moved to 5
Alpha Chapel as his SOMR.  On the 30 January 2019 a decision was made
to class 5 Alpha Chapel as his SOMR with effect from the 25 September
2018 and SPD was awarded and a new demand notice issued to the
appellant.

COUNCIL TAX DECISION

Page 4 of 6
13. In summing up, it was FCC contention that the demand notice issued to the
appellant to charge a 50% premium for the period 1 May 2018 to the 23
September 2018 classing 5 Alpha Chapel as a second home was correct.
The refusal of the Class J exemption was also correct as the appellant did
not reside at 5 Alpha Chapel as his SOMR as he had left the property to
care for his father.  He also was already caring for his father when he took
on the tenancy at 5 Alpha Chapel.

Summary of the Appellant’s Evidence

14. The appellant told the Tribunal that at the age of 21 he was living at his
mother’s house in Flint, his parents having separated.  Soon after his father
became ill and was diagnosed with Multiple Sclerosis (MS).  His father
became wheelchair bound and he moved in with his father as a live-in
carer.  He explained that he had been caring for his father for 10 years.

15. The appellant stated that 2 years ago he went to see the Doctor regarding
a stress related illness, and he was advised that it would be a great benefit
for him to get his own place to unwind.  Previously he had returned to his
mother’s house when he wasn’t working.

16. The appellant explained that around this time his father’s condition
deteriorated to such an extent that he required 2 people to care for him.
Although his budget was tight, he managed to get his own house and
signed the tenancy agreement for 5 Alpha Chapel.

17. Mr Bedford said that having spoken to friends who were carers he was
under the impression he would qualify for an exemption from paying council
tax.  He had applied online to FCC but was told he didn’t qualify and a
month or so later was notified he would also have to pay a 50% premium
on top of the council tax.  He told the Tribunal that 5 Alpha Chapel was not
a holiday home he was using it as a place to go during any holidays, illness
etc. from his work.

18. The appellant informed the Tribunal that he had got another full-time job at
TNT working nights and had attended the Tribunal straight from finishing
his night shift.  He said that it had taken 6 months of emailing back and
forth in order to get the 50% charge removed as he had returned to live at 5
Alpha Chapel.  He had gone to seek advice from the CAB in Holywell
regarding his predicament and was informed that the premium was
charged on unfurnished empty properties.

19. Mr Bedford told the Tribunal that he wasn’t a rich man, and the premium
was for rich people with money to purchase a second home.  Mr Bedford
said that he was angry with FCC as they had forced him to give up his job
caring for his father.  Soon after he’d stopped caring for his father he had
fallen and broken his arm.  The appellant believed it would not have
happened if he had been there and he felt very angry and guilty about the
situation.

COUNCIL TAX DECISION

Page 5 of 6

20. The appellant was asked by the Tribunal how long he had been caring for
his father before he moved into 5 Alpha Chapel in the first instance.  The
appellant answered 10 years and that all his bills etc. used to go to his
mother’s property, although he spent most of his time at his father’s house.

21. The Tribunal Chairwoman asked the appellant if he had said everything
that he wanted, to which he answered yes.

22. At the conclusion of the hearing the Tribunal decided to reserve its
decision.

The Reasons for Decision

23. Having considered all the evidence placed before it, both written and oral,
the Tribunal decided to dismiss the appeal for the following reasons.

24. In reaching its decision the Tribunal had regard to the prevailing legislation,
the Council Tax (Exempt Dwellings) Order 1992 (SI 1992/558) and Section
12B and Section 139 of the Housing (Wales) Act 2014.

25. It had to decide initially if FCC had acted correctly in refusing the appellant
the Class J exemption.  Secondly, it had to decide if FCC had correctly
applied the premium for a long-term empty dwelling on 5 Alpha Chapel, in
line with their statutory duty.

26. The Tribunal had regard to the qualifying criteria for a Class J, as reproduced
below: -

Extract
“….
3. A dwelling is an exempt dwelling for the purposes of section 4 of the Act on a
particular day if on that day it falls within one of the following classes –

……..
Class an unoccupied dwelling which was previously the sole or main residence of a
J:
qualifying person who –
(a) has his sole or main residence in another place for the purpose of providing,
or better providing, person care for a person who requires such care by
reason of old age, disablement, illness, past or present alcohol or drug
dependence or past or present mental disorder; and
(b) has been a relevant absentee for the whole of the period since the dwelling
last ceased to be his residence……….”

COUNCIL TAX DECISION

Page 6 of 6
27. Having considered the criteria the Tribunal decided the appellant did not
reside at 5 Alpha Chapel, as his sole or main residence, and did not leave
that property to care for his father.  The reality was that he had left his
mother’s property in Flint to care for his father and this place was regarded
as his SOMR.  Unfortunately for the appellant, since he was already caring
for his father when he took on the tenancy of 5 Alpha Chapel the Tribunal
considered that the Billing Authority was correct not to award the Class J
exemption to the subject property.

28. As regards to the charge of the 50% premium, the Tribunal believed 5
Alpha Chapel fell within the definition of a long-term empty dwelling as
prescribed in legislation.  Therefore, in its opinion, Flintshire County Council
had correctly exercised its discretion in applying the 50% premium for the
period 1 May 2018 to 23 September 2018 in this case.

29. Although the Tribunal had considerable sympathy for the appellant, it had
no option but to conform with the statutory provisions.

30. In light of the above, the Tribunal decided it had no option but to dismiss
the appeal.

TRIBIWNLYS PRISIO CYMRU - VALUATION TRIBUNAL FOR WALES

COUNCIL TAX DECISION

Page 1 of 5

Appellant: Mr M Walker

Appeal Number:  6810M12/CTL/1

Appellant’s Address: Glanaber, Main Streert, Llwyngwril LL37 2YQ

The Matter Appealed against:  Council Tax Liability Appeal

Date of Hearing: 30 May 2019

Appearances:  Mrs B Rees Gwynedd Council (GC)

Date of Decision:    17 June 2019

Decision of Tribunal:  Appeal Allowed

Members of the Tribunal:
Mr Rh Prytherch

Mr C Newman
Ms M Griffith

Tribunal Clerk: Mrs C Jones

Introduction:

1. The appellant appealed against GC’s refusal to grant him Single Person
Discount (SPD) in respect of the property Glanaber, Main Street,
Llwyngwyril.

2. This is a summary of the case and is not intended to be an exhaustive
record of the proceedings. However, the parties can be assured all the
evidence was fully considered by the Tribunal when it arrived at its
decision. Consequently, the absence of reference to any statement, or
evidence, should not be construed as being overlooked.

Summary of the Appellant’s Evidence

3. The Clerk explained that the appellant was not present and had submitted
a written submission, to read to the Tribunal in his absence.  The Clerk
then read out relevant details from the appeal form and the written
submission as reproduced below;

Extract
“I live in Llwyngwril full-time.  I own jointly with my wife, Jill Walker, two
other properties.  32 Plas Panteidal, Aberdovey, LL35 0RF is a self-
catering holiday let and 14 Hillaries Road, Erdington, Birmingham is an
HMO divided into 6 rooms with shared facilities.  No. 32 has business
rates applied and full Council Tax is paid at No 14.  Gwynedd Council
accept I live in Llwyngwril alone but say that because I am married, it is
expected that I live with my wife at No14.  It is deemed our family home.

COUNCIL TAX DECISION

Page 2 of 5
My wife works full time in Birmingham and lives at No 14 as a live-in
landlord.  I spend 0% time at No 32 and No 14 Hillaries Road will not be a
family home for me or anyone else in the future.  I will never live there
again, and my wife can’t wait to retire in roughly 2 years’ time and move to
Llwyngwril.  My GP and Dentist are in Gwynedd (Tywyn and Dolgellau).  I
vote in Gwynedd.  I run a B&B in Gwynedd.  www.glanaberbnb.co.uk  I
am 6 years older than my wife, so pension rules differ.  My wife’s GP,
Dentist, voting and banking are in Birmingham – she works and lives
there.  My banking, pensions and tax affairs are in Gwynedd.  I know this
situation is unusual, but it is genuine and temporary.  Thanks for
considering this application for Council Tax single person reduction.

………I have received a pack of information from the Council today.   I
would be grateful if this email could also be shared with the valuation
tribunal.  I have guests staying at the B&B so am unable to attend.

The Council have quoted case law that does not apply to my
situation.  The marital main residence ended in January 2016 when work
began to convert 14 Hillaries Road into an HMO.  Tenants moved in to No
14 in August 2016 and it became a small HMO with 4 unrelated people
living there.  On 1 November 2018 it became a licensed HMO with 6
unrelated people living there.

I move that the marital main residence cannot be deemed as No 14 due
to the change of use.  The marital main residence has not been re-
established and can only be done when Mrs Walker moves to Glanaber in
the near future.”

Summary of the Billing Authority’s Evidence

4. Mrs Rees on behalf of GC distributed her evidence pack to the Tribunal
which contained the following: -

• Skeleton Argument
• Supporting Evidence: -
o Appendix 1 - Land Registry entry - Glanaber, Llwyngwril
o Appendix 2 - Land Registry entry – 14 Hillaries Road, Erdington
o Appendix 3 - Cox v London South West Valuation Tribunal HC
(RVR 1994 171)
o Appendix 4 – SI 2015/2068 The Council Tax (Exceptions to
Higher Amounts) (Wales) Regulations 2015

5. Mrs Rees said that Mr Walker had been registered for Council Tax liability
at Glanaber, Llwyngwril since the 14 August 2015 together with Mrs Jill
Walker.  Mr and Mrs Walker also jointly owned the leasehold of 14 Hillaries
Road, Erdington, Birmingham.

6. Mrs Rees explained that in accordance with the Local Government Finance
Act 1992 if there was only one-person resident in the property, as their sole

COUNCIL TAX DECISION

Page 3 of 5
or main residence, a discount of 25% was applicable.  GC contended that
as this discount could only be applied to a person’s sole or main residence,
it was important to look at the sole or main residence of both Mr and Mrs
Walker and to consider relevant case law.

7. Mrs Rees quoted the case of Cox v London South West Valuation and
Community Charge Tribunal and Poole Borough Council Community
Charge Registration Officer 1994 as relevant to the appeal.  The
taxpayer spent time at two dwellings.  The High Court concluded that the
sole or main residence was the home where the wife and family resided.  It
was GC’s contention that as Mr and Mrs Walker remained in a marital
relationship it would follow, in line with the Cox v London South West case,
that either Glanaber or 14 Hillaries Road would be the sole or main
residence of both parties as the marital home.  Mr and Mrs Walker were
joint owners of both properties, therefore had security of tenure at both
addresses.

8. Mrs Rees stated that Mrs Walker had never had her sole or main residence
at the Llwyngwril address and therefore it was reasonable to assume the
marital home remained to be 14 Hillaries Road as the sole or main
residence of both Mr and Mrs Walker.  Mrs Rees acknowledged Mrs
Walker’s intention to move to Llwyngwril in a couple of years when she
retired.

9. She clarified that Mr Walker resided at the Llwyngwril as he ran a Bed and
Breakfast business from that property and consequently was required to be
on site for his guests.  This would mean that Glanaber could be a second
property, but it qualified for exception to the premium charge as a job-
related hereditament under Class 7 of SI 2015/2068 (the Council Tax
(Exceptions to Higher Amounts) (Wales) Regulations) until such time as
Mrs Walker retired and moved to Llwyngwril.

10. In conclusion of her evidence Mrs Rees said that as Mr and Mrs Walker
remained in a marital relationship, for the purposes of Council Tax and in
consideration of Council Tax case law, their sole or main residence should
be together at the same address.  It was GC’s belief that in this instance it
was reasonable to assume that this remained to be 14 Hillaries Road until
Mrs Walker ceased employment and completed the move to reside
permanently at Llwyngwril in the future.  She requested that the appeal be
dismissed.

11. At the conclusion of the hearing the Tribunal decided to reserve its
decision.

The Reasons for Decision

12. Having considered all the evidence placed before it, both written and oral,
the Tribunal decided to allow the appeal for the following reasons.

COUNCIL TAX DECISION

Page 4 of 5
13. Under the prevailing Legislation the Tribunal had to determine which
property was Mr Walker’s ‘main residence’.  It had regard to the hierarchy of
liability under Section 6 of the LGFA 1992 and concluded that a person can
only have their sole or main residence at one address.

14. Section 6(5) of the Local Government Finance Act 1992 defines the ‘resident’
of a dwelling as being an individual who has attained the age of 18 and has
his, or her, sole or main residence there. The term ‘sole or main residence’
was not defined under Statute; therefore, the Tribunal had regard to
judgements of the higher Courts in which the concept of sole or main
residence had been rehearsed on previous occasions.

15. Looking to the case law provided by the Billing Authority, the Tribunal
accepted that there were similarities.  However, unlike the Cox v London
case, in this case it was not the husband who stayed at a property due to
work commitments, but the wife.

16. The Tribunal believed that a marital home could be established elsewhere,
if the appellants chose to do so, keeping the original property for the
partner’s work commitments.

17. Focusing on the material facts of Mr Walker’ situation, the Tribunal concluded
that he had stronger links to the Llwyngwril property.  He ran a bed and
breakfast business there, so he had work links there.  He had no work links
to the Birmingham address.    Mr Walker’s driving licence was registered to
the Llwyngwril address as was his bank account.  He was registered with a
Doctor and Dentist and registered to vote in Gwynedd.  Mr Walker had
indicated that he had no intention of returning to live at his former marital
home in Birmingham.  This fact was supported by the conversion of this
property into a registered house in multiple occupation.  The intention was
for Mrs Walker to retire to the Llwyngwril address and join her husband within
the next two years.

18. In the Tribunal’s opinion, whilst 4 Hillaries Road was previously the couple’s
matrimonial home and where his wife continued to live, the property was now
an HMO and occupied by several other residents.

19. The Tribunal, in the absence of any other argument, accepted that Mr
Walker intended to stay at the Llwyngwril address.  It was accepted that he
spent all his time at Llwyngwril.

20. Based on the balance of probability the Tribunal felt the Mr Walker’s sole or
main residence lay in Gwynedd, and not in Birmingham.

21. Looking to the scope of the appeal the Tribunal felt that it had no remit,
under this appeal, to decide on Mrs Walker’s sole or main residence.  The
matter under consideration was whether Gwynedd Council had acted
correctly in denying Mr Walker the Single Person’s Discount at the
Llwyngwril address.

COUNCIL TAX DECISION

Page 5 of 5
22. Considering the above, the Tribunal concluded that Mr Walker’s work and
financial links together with the pattern of family life would indicate that
Glanaber, Main Streert, Llwyngwril was the appellant’s ‘main residence’.
Therefore, Gwynedd Council were incorrect in refusing the Single Person’s
Discount.
